column51: During this period, the ACT Government’s website indicated that buses and light rail services continued to run their regular schedule, with additional services added to help with social distancing. column24: During this period, there were no mandated workplace closings. However, the ACT Government’s Canberra Recovery Plan did impose some restrictions on gathering and density limits in businesses and venues as part of their stage 4 restrictions.   These included density limits of 25 people or of one person per two square metres of useable space indoors and outdoors provided the Check In CBR app was used to collect patron details. Where the Check In CBR app was not used, density limits of one person per four square metres of usable space indoors and one person per two square metres of usable space outdoors remained in effect.   Additionally, large indoor performance venues, enclosed outdoor venues, cinemas and movie theatres, as well as GIO Stadium and Manuka Oval were allowed up to 65% of capacity (restricted) provided additional COVID restrictions were adhered to.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210517104956/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/news-articles/update-heading-back-to-work  https://web.archive.org/web/20210119015152/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/what-you-can-do

column88: Get tested for COVID-19 if you have any of the following symptoms, no matter how mild:    A fever of 37.5 degrees or higher, or recent history of fever such as chills or night sweats, OR  Symptoms of a respiratory infection, such as sore throat, cough, runny or blocked nose, or shortness of breath, OR  Loss of sense of smell or taste.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210517130348/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested/when-to-get-tested
column90: Contact tracing policy:  If your result is positive, ACT Health will contact you and give you advice about what you need to do.    ACT Health will also work to identify people you may have had contact with while you were infectious.    ACT Health and your health care professional will work out if you need be in hospital or can recover safely at home.    ACT Health will call your contacts and provide them with advice, including what they need to do if they develop symptoms.    You must remain in isolation until ACT Health advises you that it’s safe to return to normal activities.    ACT Health will contact you regularly while you are in isolation.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210517132154/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/symptoms-and-getting-tested/when-you-get-your-result

column115: People who have been to a geographical area of risk should not visit or work in high-risk settings, including aged care facilities and hospitals, for a period of 14 days after leaving these area. This advice extends to staff, volunteers and visitors to high-risk settings.    Visitors cannot visit aged care facilities if they:  have returned from overseas in the last 14 days.  have been in a geographical area of risk in the last 14 days.  have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days.  have a temperature higher than 37.5 degrees or history of fever (e.g. night sweats or chills).  symptoms of a respiratory infection such as a cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, loss of smell or loss of taste.    Residents can have no more than two people visiting at any one time.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210117200824/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/aged-care/advice-for-visitors-to-aged-care-facilities

column69: Travel restriction remain in place for 11 specific COVID-19 affected Local Government Areas in Sydney, NSW. ACT residents in those areas can return to the ACT, but need to notify ACT Health of their intention to return via our online declaration form and enter quarantine for 14 days.  Non-ACT residents in those areas are legally not permitted to enter the ACT without a valid exemption. If people who have been in these areas in the last 14 days need to travel to the ACT for extraordinary circumstances, they need to apply for an exemption at least three days prior to their travel. We urge people from these areas to not travel to the ACT at this time.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210507033318/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/news-articles/travel-restrictions-currently-in-place-in-the-act

The Northern Beaches Local Government Area (LGA) will today be removed from the list of COVID-19 affected LGAs in Sydney. However a Public Health Direction still remains in place for 10 LGAs in Western and South-western Sydney, NSW. The travel restriction remains the same.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210507040532/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/news-articles/northern-beaches-no-longer-a-covid-19-affected-area

column15: According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported.    However, visitor numbers at schools could not exceed 1000 individuals, and visitors were required to follow a density rule of 1 person per 2 square metres in all indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as use the Check in CBR app.    Normal school activities such as assemblies were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metres, which applied up to 1000 individuals with check-in procedures in place.     Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited.    The directions in place between April and May 2021 were a continuation of existing restrictions. column24: According to the ACT Government website (as last updated on 11 May and 12 April 2021), there was no mention of a requirement for businesses to close. However, businesses had to follow some COVID-safe restrictions in order to operate:    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above. COVID safety plans were required for all venues, as well as individual events with over 500 individuals attending, which also needed to notify ACT Health before commencing.    All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. All performances and cultural events were required to be ticketed, and cultural events attended by over 5000 individuals in a single areas needed to be ticketed and seated.    Performers were required to be at least 2 metres away from their audiences and 1.5 metres away from other performers. Conductors, instructors, and accompanists were required to be at least 2 metres away from other performers.    Dancing was considered a high-risk activity in licensed venues, which needed to designate specific areas for dancing, and set capacity limits on dancefloors based on the 'one person per two square metres' rule.    Guided tours needed to be shorter than 2 hours, and gaming machines needed to be spaced at least 1.5 metres apart.    The directions in place between April and May 2021 were a continuation of existing directions. column15: According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported.    However, visitor numbers at schools could not exceed 1000 individuals, and visitors were required to follow a density rule of 1 person per 2 square metres in all indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as use the Check in CBR app.    Normal school activities such as assemblies were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metres, which applied up to 1000 individuals with check-in procedures in place.     Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited.    The directions in place between April and May 2021 were a continuation of existing restrictions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210427043718/https://www.education.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/1714320/COVID-19-Placemat-for-publication-1-March-2021.pdf  https://www.education.act.gov.au/public-school-life/covid-school-arrangements
column24: According to the ACT Government website (as last updated on 11 May and 12 April 2021), there was no mention of a requirement for businesses to close. However, businesses had to follow some COVID-safe restrictions in order to operate:    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above. COVID safety plans were required for all venues, as well as individual events with over 500 individuals attending, which also needed to notify ACT Health before commencing.    All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. All performances and cultural events were required to be ticketed, and cultural events attended by over 5000 individuals in a single areas needed to be ticketed and seated.    Performers were required to be at least 2 metres away from their audiences and 1.5 metres away from other performers. Conductors, instructors, and accompanists were required to be at least 2 metres away from other performers.    Dancing was considered a high-risk activity in licensed venues, which needed to designate specific areas for dancing, and set capacity limits on dancefloors based on the 'one person per two square metres' rule.    Guided tours needed to be shorter than 2 hours, and gaming machines needed to be spaced at least 1.5 metres apart.    The directions in place between 8 and 21 May 2021 were a continuation of existing directions. column115: No new policy for aged care facilities. Visitors providing a care and support visit to a resident are no longer required to have a 2020 influenza vaccine to enter a residential aged care facility. Visitors providing a care and support visit include a spouse, family member, close relative, friend or carer. Staff, contractors, volunteers, people providing goods and services (including health services), and prospective residents are still required to have received the 2020 influenza vaccine prior to entering a residential aged care facility.  People who have been to a geographical area of risk should not visit or work in high-risk settings, including aged care facilities and hospitals, for a period of 14 days after leaving these area. This advice extends to staff, volunteers and visitors to high-risk settings.   While the Public Health Emergency is in place in the ACT, the only people permitted at a residential aged care facility in the ACT are:  •	A current or prospective resident of the facility.  •	An employee or contractor of the residential aged care facility.  •	A person whose presence at the premises is for the purposes of providing:  o	Goods or services that are necessary for the effective operation of the residential aged care facility.  o	Health, medical or pharmaceutical goods or services to a resident of the residential aged care facility.  o	Care and support to a resident of the residential aged care facility.  o	End of life support for a resident of the residential aged care facility.  o	Emergency management or law enforcement.  This allows for the visiting a family member or close friend in an aged care facility for the purposes of providing care and support. There is no limit to the number of hours to a visit.  Visitors cannot visit aged care facilities if they:  •	Have returned from overseas in the last 14 days.  •	Have been in a geographical area of risk in the last 14 days.  •	Have been in contact with a confirmed case of COVID-19 in the last 14 days.  •	Have a temperature higher than 37.5 degrees or history of fever (e.g. night sweats or chills).  •	Symptoms of a respiratory infection such as a cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, loss of smell or loss of taste.  Web archived: http://web.archive.org/web/20210423082111/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/aged-care/advice-for-visitors-to-aged-care-facilities

column15: According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported.    However, visitor numbers at schools could not exceed 1000 individuals, and visitors were required to follow a density rule of 1 person per 2 square metres in all indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as use the Check in CBR app.    Normal school activities such as assemblies were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metres, which applied up to 1000 individuals with check-in procedures in place.     Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited.    The directions in place between April and May 2021 were a continuation of existing restrictions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210427043718/https://www.education.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/1714320/COVID-19-Placemat-for-publication-1-March-2021.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20210416152528/https://www.education.act.gov.au/public-school-life/covid-school-arrangements  https://web.archive.org/web/20210627101849/https://www.education.act.gov.au/public-school-life/covid-school-arrangements
column24: According to the ACT Government website (as last updated on 11 May and 12 April 2021), there was no mention of a requirement for businesses to close. However, businesses had to follow some COVID-safe restrictions in order to operate:    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above. COVID safety plans were required for all venues, as well as individual events with over 500 individuals attending, which also needed to notify ACT Health before commencing.    All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. All performances and cultural events were required to be ticketed, and cultural events attended by over 5000 individuals in a single areas needed to be ticketed and seated.    Performers were required to be at least 2 metres away from their audiences and 1.5 metres away from other performers. Conductors, instructors, and accompanists were required to be at least 2 metres away from other performers.    Dancing was considered a high-risk activity in licensed venues, which needed to designate specific areas for dancing, and set capacity limits on dancefloors based on the 'one person per two square metres' rule.    Guided tours needed to be shorter than 2 hours, and gaming machines needed to be spaced at least 1.5 metres apart.    The directions in place between 22 and 31 May 2021 were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210627103453/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/business-and-work/cafes,-restaurants-and-other-hospitality/what-your-venue-or-business-needs-to-do#Register-for-and-use-the-Check-In-CBR-app  http://web.archive.org/web/20210627103457/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/business-and-work/entertainment-live-performance-arts-cultural-activities/what-your-venue-or-business-needs-to-do  http://web.archive.org/web/20210414025855/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/business-and-work/cafes,-restaurants-and-other-hospitality/what-your-venue-or-business-needs-to-do
column33: According to the Public Health (Restricted Activities – Gatherings, Business or Undertakings) Emergency Direction 2021 (No 3) which was in place between 14 April 2021 and 1 July 2021, individual events with over 500 attendees were required to develop and follow a COVID-19 Safety Plan and follow directions set out in the COVID Safe Event Protocol. The protocol  included a one person per two square metre rule for both indoor and outdoor events, was well as further directions  for specific event types such as outdoor music festivals, which were required to be ticketed and seated events where dancing was only permitted in front of seats. Events which offered rides or were held at amusement parks also needed to maintain increased cleaning in high-touch areas.    Events with over 1000 attendees were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption in order to go ahead, as well as follow the directions outlined in the Public Health (Restricted Activities – Gatherings, Business or Undertakings) Emergency Direction 2021 (No 3).    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above.     The directions in place between 22 and 31 May 2021 were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220306222531/https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/DownloadFile/ni/2021-216/20210414-76274/PDF/2021-216.PDF  http://web.archive.org/web/20210627103457/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/business-and-work/entertainment-live-performance-arts-cultural-activities/what-your-venue-or-business-needs-to-do
column51: According to the Transport Canberra website as of 26 April and 22 July 2021, hard surfaces at bus interchanges and light rail stops were cleaned daily, and surfaces inside buses and light rail vehicles were cleaned twice daily. As a COVID-19 safety precaution, buses did not accept cash payments and the 2021 public transport network was upgraded to support more off-peak travel. Passengers were also prohibited from sitting on the front seat of buses, and were asked to enter buses using the rear doors in order to keep bus drivers safe.    Maintaining a physical distance of 1.5m and maintaining good hand hygiene was recommended.    The directions in place between 22 and 31 May 2021 were a continuation of existing directions. column79: The ACT introduced a range of actions and providing practical support, such as rebates and the freezing of some government fees to reduce pressure on household budgets.  Residential rates - The usual annual increase will not be applied to 2020-21 general rates bills. This combined with a $150 rebate to the fixed charge component of all 2020-21 residential rates bills means average residential general rates will not increase. Rates will reduce for around two-thirds of homeowners. Some homeowners will notice an increase due to their land value going up.  The government has also frozen the Fire and Emergency Services Levy in 2020-21 at the current 2019-20 level.   The ACT Revenue Office will implement a new process for rates deferrals for owner occupiers experiencing hardship because of COVID-19. No interest will apply to the deferred amount.  The deferral will be for 12 months where household income has been significantly (at least 25%) reduced by circumstances such as:  •	unemployment  •	reduction in hours of work  •	a loss of small business income.  Eligibility criteria will include income testing (household incomes less than $160,000 before tax).  As part of COVID-19 responses, an additional one-off $200 was provided to Utilities Concession holders towards the end of 2020-21.  This includes: Centrelink Pensioner Concession Card holders, Centrelink Low Income Health Care Card holders and Veteran’s Affairs Pensioner Concession Card or Gold Card holders.   The Government is providing land tax and rates rebates to landlords of residential properties who reduce rents by at least 25 per cent for tenants impacted by COVID-19.   The rebate will be equal to 50 per cent of the rent reduction, capped at $1,300 per quarter (around $100 per week), until 30 June 2021. This will provide rental relief to impacted tenants of up to $200 per week. Archived link http://web.archive.org/web/20210613150327/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/community/families-and-households

column15: According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported.    However, visitor numbers at schools could not exceed 1000 individuals, and visitors were required to follow a density rule of 1 person per 2 square metres in all indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as use the Check in CBR app.    Normal school activities such as assemblies were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metres, which applied up to 1000 individuals with check-in procedures in place.     Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited.    The directions in place during 15-27 June 2021 were a continuation of existing restrictions. column24: According to the ACT Government website (as of 27 June 2021 and last updated on 11 May and 12 April 2021), there was no mention of a requirement for businesses to close. However, businesses had to follow some COVID-safe restrictions in order to operate:    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above. COVID safety plans were required for all venues, as well as individual events with over 500 individuals attending, which also needed to notify ACT Health before commencing.    All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. All performances and cultural events were required to be ticketed, and cultural events attended by over 5000 individuals in a single areas needed to be ticketed and seated.    Performers were required to be at least 2 metres away from their audiences and 1.5 metres away from other performers. Conductors, instructors, and accompanists were required to be at least 2 metres away from other performers.    Dancing was considered a high-risk activity in licensed venues, which needed to designate specific areas for dancing, and set capacity limits on dancefloors based on the 'one person per two square metres' rule.    Guided tours needed to be shorter than 2 hours, and gaming machines needed to be spaced at least 1.5 metres apart.    The directions in place between 15 and 27 June 2021 were a continuation of existing directions. The protocol  included a one person per two square metre rule for both indoor and outdoor events, was well as further directions  for specific event types such as outdoor music festivals, which were required to be ticketed and seated events where dancing was only permitted in front of seats. Events which offered rides or were held at amusement parks also needed to maintain increased cleaning in high-touch areas.    Events with over 1000 attendees were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption in order to go ahead, as well as follow the directions outlined in the Public Health (Restricted Activities – Gatherings, Business or Undertakings) Emergency Direction 2021 (No 3). As part of COVID-19 responses, an additional one-off $200 was provided to Utilities Concession holders towards the end of 2020-21.  This includes: Centrelink Pensioner Concession Card holders, Centrelink Low Income Health Care Card holders and Veteran’s Affairs Pensioner Concession Card or Gold Card holders.   The Government is providing land tax and rates rebates to landlords of residential properties who reduce rents by at least 25 per cent for tenants impacted by COVID-19.   The rebate will be equal to 50 per cent of the rent reduction, capped at $1,300 per quarter (around $100 per week), until 30 June 2021. column103: No policy change. Under a public health direction effective from 11.59pm on Friday 22 January 2021, face masks are mandatory for people aged 12 and over, including workers who interact with the public, while inside the Canberra Airport terminal and during domestic commercial flights in and out of Canberra. Although face masks are not required to be worn outside the terminal of Canberra Airport, passengers embarking and disembarking a flight on the tarmac must keep them on.  There are some exceptions, including:  •	Infants and children under 12 years  •	People with a medical condition or disability which makes wearing a mask unsuitable  •	During an emergency  •	When eating, drinking or taking medication  •	When removing the mask is required for communicating effectively, for example, with someone who is hard of hearing  •	When wearing a mask is a risk to health and safety  •	When someone’s identity needs to be confirmed, for example, through security gates  •	Airport workers and air crew who are not interacting directly with passengers or members of the public.  Face masks must be designed or made to be worn over the mouth and nose and should fit securely around your face to provide the wearer with protection against infection. A scarf or bandana is not considered an appropriate face mask.  Archived link http://web.archive.org/web/20210626050410/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/protect-yourself#Masks
column106: All people in phase 1a, 1b, people aged 40 years and over, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 16 years and over, are currently being vaccinated. This includes those who:  •	are most vulnerable to the effects of COVID-19  •	have the highest risk of being exposed to the virus  •	have the highest risk of spreading the virus  Phase 1a started on 22 February 2021.  During phase 1a, the vaccine has been given to:  •	quarantine and border workers  •	health care workers working in high-risk exposure and transmission areas, like COVID-19 testing clinics, respiratory clinics and some emergency department staff  •	residents and staff of aged care and disability residential care facilities  Phase 1b started on 22 March 2021.  People in phase 1b include:  •	people aged 70 years and over  •	all health care workers, including aged and disability care  •	Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 years and older  •	people aged 16 and over with an underlying medical condition*  •	people aged 16 and over with disability  •	critical and high-risk workers  •	household contacts of quarantine and border workers  •	other eligible individuals like:  •	carers of people in 1a and 1b  •	carers of children with underlying medical conditions  •	disability and aged care support volunteer   Web link: http://web.archive.org/web/20210626050345/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/vaccine/when-will-i-get-the-covid-19-vaccine

column15: According to the Public Health (Mandatory Face Masks) Emergency Direction 2021, the ACT Government imposed a mask mandate which required individuals aged 12 years old and above to carry and wear a face mask in or at any business or undertaking. This mandate came into effect at 11:59pm on 27 July 2021, and was a tightening of existing COVID-19 restrictions.    All other directions pertaining to schools remained the same:    According to a March 2021 ACT Government publication which outlined how schools would operate in 2021, students and staff were expected to continue on-campus learning, although remote learning for students vulnerable to COVID-19 was supported.    However, visitor numbers at schools could not exceed 1000 individuals, and visitors were required to follow a density rule of 1 person per 2 square metres in all indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as use the Check in CBR app.    Normal school activities such as assemblies were required to follow a 1 person per 2 square metres, which applied up to 1000 individuals with check-in procedures in place.     Additional school events (such as concerts and fetes) with more than 1000 people attending were required to successfully apply for an exemption in order to go ahead. ACT Health had to be notified of events with 501-1000 people attending, and a COVID-safety plan for these events was required to be submitted in order for them to run.    Regular cleaning of shared surfaces was conducted on top of routine cleaning, and all schools were provided with hand sanitiser.    Offsite events and carnivals were required to follow COVID Safe event protocols. School camps and excursions held overseas or in identified COVID-19 affected areas interstate were prohibited. column24: According to the Public Health (Mandatory Face Masks) Emergency Direction 2021, the ACT Government imposed a mask mandate which required individuals aged 12 years old and above to carry and wear a face mask in or at any business or undertaking. This mandate came into effect at 11:59pm on 27 July 2021, and was a tightening of existing COVID-19 restrictions.    All other directions pertaining to businesses the same:    According to the ACT Government website (as of 27 June 2021 and last updated on 11 May and 12 April 2021), there was no mention of a requirement for businesses to close. However, businesses had to follow some COVID-safe restrictions in order to operate:    Businesses were required to register for the Check in CBR contact tracing system, and collect contact information from staff and patrons aged 16 years old and above. COVID safety plans were required for all venues, as well as individual events with over 500 individuals attending, which also needed to notify ACT Health before commencing.    All events in the hospitality sector attended by over 1000 individuals were required to successfully apply for a COVID exemption. All performances and cultural events were required to be ticketed, and cultural events attended by over 5000 individuals in a single areas needed to be ticketed and seated.    Performers were required to be at least 2 metres away from their audiences and 1.5 metres away from other performers. Conductors, instructors, and accompanists were required to be at least 2 metres away from other performers.    Dancing was considered a high-risk activity in licensed venues, which needed to designate specific areas for dancing, and set capacity limits on dancefloors based on the 'one person per two square metres' rule.    Guided tours needed to be shorter than 2 hours, and gaming machines needed to be spaced at least 1.5 metres apart. column42: Gathering sizes at most non-essential businesses are limited to 25 people, and in addition there is a maximum density of 1 person per 2 square metres. column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418. - The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments  https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment

column77: -	People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 7 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments.

Some examples included on the NSW COVID-19 webpage include rent decrease relief for home-owners and also rent relief. These schemes were available for all NSW residents.     These policies were in place for much of the pandemic and had not be changed during this time period.    Financial support webpage:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210720014939/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/financial-support
column86: According to COVID-19 case statistics from Mar 2020 found on the archived link, it is assumed that NSW's primary COVID-19 public information campaign began at this time. column88: According to the archived link from NSW's COVID-19 campaign page, testing was available and encourage to anyone in NSW who was symptomatic during this time period. Testing facilities were not freely available for some communities, especially rural and remote communities in NSW. There was no update on increased testing during this period, so it is assumed that the archived link doesnt represent a tightening or relaxing of restrictions. column90: The NSW government mapped out in detail their approach to contact tracing in an announcement on Nov 22nd 2020. This announcement described how they utilise the mandatory electronic check in app, as well as public health surveillance of close contacts of cases. These methods were in place for contact tracing over the whole of NSW.    This announcement represents an increasingly enhanced approach to contact tracing.     It is assumed from data that these methods were in place throughout this whole time period.    Announcement:   https://web.archive.org/web/20210426095244/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/surveillance-plan.aspx
column103: As per the NSW legislative registrar on Apr 1st 2021, a new order was to commence at midnight on this date with updated mandatory mask wearing settings. NSW airports were now the only mandatory place for mask wearing. This applied to the whole of NSW.    Prior to this order, masks were mandatory on public transport in some parts of NSW. Thus, this order represented a relaxation of restrictions.    This policy remained in in place throughout this whole time period and until May 6th 2021.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210728064410/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20%28COVID-19%20Mandatory%20Face%20Coverings%29%20Order%20%28No%202%29%202021.pdf
column106: As announced by the Australian Government department of health on Mar 22nd 2021, phase 1b of the Australian national vaccine rollout commenced from midnight of this date. This included 3 core groups, plus additional groups: 80 years and over; 70-79 year olds, other healthcare workers, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people over 55 years old, adults with an underlying medical condition, including those with a disability, critical and high risk workers. Both the Pfizer and Astrazeneca vaccine was available to these groups. NSW was to follow the national vaccine rollout, and the above mentioned vaccines was available at various settings across the whole of NSW for the eligible groups.     This phase of the rollout represented and increased availability of vaccines to residents in NSW, representing a strengthening in vaccine policy.    This phase was in place for the whole time period, and the next phase was due to commence in early May 2021.    Phase 1b announcement:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210427010008/https://www.health.gov.au/resources/publications/covid-19-vaccination-phase-1b-rollout
column115: As published on the NSW legislative registrar on Mar 10th 2021, aged care policy that was in place in NSW had been repealed without amendment. The amendment order (first archived link) advised the aged care facility operators must consider the advice of the health minister in areas such as employee screening, face mask use and influenza + COVID-19 vaccination requirements. Some details for these areas were provided in the second archived link, however it was unclear what the amended policy enforced for aged care facilities. The repealed order was in action for the whole of NSW.    As it was unclear what order was in place for the time period, it is difficult to state whether aged care restrictions had been tightened or loosened during this period.     There was no specific aged care policy in place for this whole time period, and according to the NSW legislative registrar no new aged care policies have been brought in. column77: Between 7 april and 13 april, some forms of income supports are available. According to the Services Australia website (Last update 30 March 2021) "The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) is a one-off payment if you’re affected by coronavirus (COVID-19). To get this you must be: eligible for an income support payment or ABSTUDY Living Allowance; in severe financial hardship; in Australia when you claim".  There is also a "Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment" for those who can't earn an income because they must self-isolate or quarantine themselves, or are caring for someone with COVID-19". Eligible persons will receive $1,500 for each 14 day period of isolation/quarantine, or when caring for someone with COVID-19". column33: There were no new policies targeting public events introduced during this period.     As published on the NSW legislative registrar on Mar 29th 2021, new restrictions were introduced commencing at 11:59pm on this date that targeted public events. All venues would now move the 1 person per 2 square metre rule, standing up would now be allowed at hospitality venues and there would be a cap for mass gatherings at 5000 people with appropriate following of specific hygiene measures. This policy was implemented across the whole of NSW.     According to a press release from NSW premier Gladys Berejiklian on Mar 26th 2021, this new policy represented an 'easing of COVID-19 related restrictions'. Key outcomes relaxed was the removal of sitting-down only at venues and also the number of people allowed in venues.     According to the NSW legislative registrar, new policy concerning public events was updated on May 3rd 2021.     Legislation:   https://web.archive.org/web/20210719022721/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20%28COVID-19%20Gathering%20Restrictions%29%20Order%202021_210409.pdf    Gladys Berejiklian announcement:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210719024042/https://www.gladys.com.au/content/covid-19-restrictions-ease-compliance-must-increase
column42: There were no new policies targeting gatherings introduced during this period. Key outcomes relaxed was the increase in amount of people allowed at a gathering, as well as no cap on the amount of visitors allowed on residence. column60: There was no new policy introduced during this time period that targeted stay at home requirements. column69: No new policy was updated during this time period specifically concerning internal movement.     Policy published on the NSW legislative registrar on Feb 4th 2021 outlines specific details targeting internal movement that was in effect during this time period. This policy states that a traveller returning to NSW from an affected area must complete a self-declaration form, and if they returned from an 'area of concern', they must complete a 14 day isolation at a place of residence. This policy applies to the whole of NSW.    This amended policy does not represent a tightening nor a relaxing of restrictions, rather just an updated version of internal movement policy in NSW. According to data, there were no places of concern flagged by the NSW government during this period.    According to the NSW legislative registrar, this policy was in effect until it was amended on May 4th 2021. column106: COVID-19 vaccines are free for everyone living in Australia.  If you are aged: 18 to 39 years old, you can ask your GP about getting the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine or book an appointment at a NSW Health vaccination clinic. column24: Commencing at 5pm on Saturday 14 August 2021, stay at home rules have been extended across all of NSW. This is a tightening of the previous policy as more areas are now subject to the stay-at-home order. People must stay at home unless they have a reasonable excuse to leave their home (listed in archived links below). Workers should work from home when reasonably able to do so.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210815122144/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/what-you-can-do-nsw   http://web.archive.org/web/20210801125336/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney#closure-of-retail-businesses   Greater Sydney: https://web.archive.org/web/20210816005424/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney    Regional NSW:   https://web.archive.org/web/20210816033029/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions
column33: The Minister directs that each adult member of a household must not allow a visitor to be at the place of residence of the household in an LGA of concern unless the visitor is an authorised worker. column42: A maximum gathering of 2 people outside is allowed. No indoor gatherings can occur for all of NSW from 14 Aug 2020. Regional NSW is now under the same restrictions as Greater Sydney. This policy is a tightening of the policy prior. https://web.archive.org/web/20210902100347/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney https://web.archive.org/web/20210901230252/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions
column60: - The NSW Government has now extended stay at home rules across all of NSW from 5pm on Saturday 14 August 2021. Residents may only leave for reasonable excuses (eg exercise, grocery shopping, education, work etc). This is a continuation of the current stay at home rules imposed since 6pm on Saturday 26 June.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210815122144/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/what-you-can-do-nsw    - From 12:01am Monday, August 16, in Greater Sydney and other lockdown areas, the 10 kilometre rule will be reduced, with shopping, exercise and outdoor recreation to be done in a person’s local government area (LGA) or, if outside their LGA, within 5 kilometres of home. LGAs of concern must still exercise and shop within 5 kilometres from home only. There are also increased penalties for breaking these rules. Moreover, in LGAs of concern, outdoor recreation is now banned.   https://web.archive.org/web/20211004024843/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/increased-fines-test-and-isolate-payments-and-new-compliance-measures-as-nsw-battles    - From 12.01am Saturday 21 August, people who live alone must now register their 'singles bubble'.   https://web.archive.org/web/20211004024843/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/increased-fines-test-and-isolate-payments-and-new-compliance-measures-as-nsw-battles    - A curfew is in place from 12:01am on August 23 2021 in the Bayside, Blacktown, Burwood, Campbelltown, Canterbury-Bankstown, Cumberland, Fairfield, Georges River, Liverpool, Parramatta, Strathfield, or some suburbs of Penrith local government areas. You cannot leave your home between 9pm and 5am unless you have a reasonable excuse. This is a tightening of current policy in response to Covid-19.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210824125240/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area
column69: On August 14, for Greater Sydney, the distance a person is generally permitted to travel outside a person’s local government area to obtain food or other goods or services or for exercise and outdoor recreation is reduced from 10 kilometres to 5 kilometres.  Do not travel to Greater Sydney without a reasonable excuse. If you live in NSW regional and rural areas, you must have a reasonable excuse to enter Greater Sydney including the Blue Mountains, Central Coast, Wollongong and Shellharbour local government areas. A person must also not enter regional and rural NSW without a reasonable excuse (reasons listed in the archived link below). Entry to NSW from another state is restricted when an NSW Health concerns notice identifies interstate hotspots, affected areas and places of concern (details in archived link).  https://web.archive.org/web/20210815093801/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions https://web.archive.org/web/20210814073131/https://gazette.legislation.nsw.gov.au/so/download.w3p?id=Gazette_2021_2021-391.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20210812062047/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/border-restrictions
column103: Face masks must now be worn by persons over 12 years in indoor areas of non-residential premises across all of NSW.    You must also wear a face mask in NSW:  at a COVID-19 safe outdoor gathering  a controlled outdoor public gathering  if you are on public transport  in a major recreation facility such as a stadium  if you are working in a hospitality venue  if you are working in indoor areas of construction sites  if you are working at or visiting a school.  There are certain exemptions to this requirement.    In areas subject to stay at home rules, masks must be worn in additional locations including:  indoor common property areas of residential premises (e.g. lifts and lobbies of apartment blocks)  indoor and outdoor areas of food markets  outdoor areas near food, drink or retail premises  outdoor areas while working.  People in areas subject to stay at home rules must carry a mask with them at all times when away from their residence.    This is a tightening of the previous policy as this policy applies to more areas than before.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210820020827/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/public-health-orders.aspx
column115: All areas of NSW are currently under stay at home Orders.    All facilities in NSW must:  exclude all visitors, except those providing essential caring functions and end of life visits.  ensure that all essential care visitors wear a surgical mask. For reasons when masks can be removed please see Additional Advice.  ensure all essential visits must be in the resident's room.    Essential visitors must not enter an RACF at all if they:  have been to any close, casual or monitor for symptoms locations in NSW in the last 14 days  have been to Victoria or the Australian Capital Territory in the past 14 days unless providing essential caring functions or for end of life visits.  have been to any close and casual contact places of high concern in Victorian, Queensland or the Australian Capital Territory.  have been in New Zealand in the last 14 days  have COVID-19 symptoms  are a close contact of a person with confirmed COVID-19 and are within their isolation period.  live in a household with a person who is currently isolating.  are waiting for a COVID-19 test result.    This is a tightening of the previous policy.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210830043934/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/racf-latest-advice.aspx

column51: The NSW Government have not closed public transport. You must wear a face mask on public transport when required by public health orders. column77: Individuals may be eligible for various types of income support. There are three main types. The 'COVID-19 Disaster Payment' is a lump sum payment to help workers unable to earn income due to a COVID-19 state or territory public health order. This may involve a lockdown, hotspot or movement restrictions. The 'Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment' and the 'Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19)' provides income support for those who are required to enter quarantine or isolation.     This is a continuation of the national policy response to COVID-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004190443/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/subjects/getting-help-during-coronavirus-covid-19/if-you-need-payment
column79: Tenants who can’t pay their rent in full because they are impacted by the recent COVID-19 outbreak are protected from eviction.    To be eligible for the protection against eviction, a tenant needs to:  show that rent paying members of the household are impacted by COVID-19 and have lost employment, work hours or income or have had to stop working because they or other members of their household (or in their care) were/are ill with COVID; and  show that the  household’s take home weekly income has reduced by 25% or more (including any government assistance received) compared to the weekly income received in the 4 weeks prior to 26 June 2021; and  continue to pay at least 25% of the rent payable.    The 60 day protection against eviction for rental arrears applies to all tenancy agreements, including informal, unwritten agreements.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210801032604/https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/resource-library/publications/coronavirus-covid-19/property/moratorium

column74: As noted by the Department of Home Affairs, between 18 August 2021 and 31 August 2021, foreign travellers are banned from entering Australia subject to limited exemptions. This means a continuation of the previous policy: Businesses providing essential products and services that can be open are listed in the archived link below. http://web.archive.org/web/20210801125336/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney#closure-of-retail-businesses     Additionally, from 12.01am Monday, 23 August, the following retail premises must close in local government areas of concern in Greater Sydney except for click and collect: garden centres and plant nurseries, office supplies, hardware and building supplies, landscaping material supplies, rural supplies, and pet supplies.   https://web.archive.org/web/20220511212046/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/new-protections-and-compliance-rules-to-carry-nsw-through-to-vaccination-targets
column60: According to a NSW Government media release published on 20 August 2021, a 9pm-5am curfew would be introduced in LGAs of concern from 12:01am on 23 August 2021. Individuals living in these LGAs could not leave home between 9pm-5am unless they were undertaking permitted work, responding to emergencies, or accessing medical care. This was a tightening of COVID-19 policy in LGAs of concern.  Other stay at home restrictions continued to apply:  According to the NSW Government website as of 23 August 2021, stay at home orders applied to all of NSW (Greater Sydney, LGAs of concern, and regional NSW). Individuals could only leave home if they had a reasonable excuse to do so. column24: According to a media release published by NSW Health on 26 August 2021, stay at home orders in place in regional NSW would be extended until 11:59pm on 10 September 2021 at the earliest. This expansion of existing government policy brought the restrictions imposed on all of rural and regional NSW in line with the restrictions placed on Greater Sydney.    As part of these restrictions, most retail premises, entertainment venues and recreational areas, places of worship, and personal care services were required to close.   Businesses which provided essential goods and services were allowed to conduct in-person operations. However, for most of NSW (areas of NSW which were not considered to be LGAs of concern), garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores were included in the list of essential businesses which were open to all. The full list of businesses which were allowed to open in Greater Sydney and regional NSW is available at the following websites:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210826121328/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20210827114420/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions    Parts of NSW (more specifically, Greater Sydney) which were considered to be LGAs of concern (Bayside, Blacktown, Burwood, Campbelltown, Canterbury-Bankstown, Cumberland, Fairfield, Georges River, Liverpool, Parramatta, Strathfield, and parts of Penrith) were required to follow more stringent restrictions. Only businesses which provided essential goods and services were allowed conduct in-person operations. Garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores were only open to relevant tradespeople. Educational and professional development activities were moved online.  The list of businesses which were allowed to operate in LGAs of concern is available at the following websites:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210828021030/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area  https://web.archive.org/web/20220511212046/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/new-protections-and-compliance-rules-to-carry-nsw-through-to-vaccination-targets     Other archived links:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210827104527/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/news/pages/20210826_00.aspx  http://web.archive.org/web/20210827225007/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/what-you-can-do-nsw

column69: According to the NSW Government website as of 25 August 2021, individuals entering NSW from interstate areas of concern, affected areas, and places of high concern (i.e. parts of Victoria, Queensland, and the ACT) were either prohibited from entering NSW or required to quarantine for 14 days upon arrival depending on the status of the area they were travelling from. column90: According to the NSW Government website (as of 8 August and 2 September 2021), businesses operating during this time were required to register as COVID-Safe and keep records of people entering their premises.     The NSW Health website (as of 25 August 2021) also published details of venues where patrons were likely to have been exposed to COVID-19. In metropolitan NSW, active contact tracing (i.e. notifying individuals who were exposed to COVID-19)  was focused on high-risk areas such as households, workplaces, healthcare and aged care facilities, childcare centres, and areas where transmission was deemed likely to occur. NSW Health continued to identify all contact locations in areas outside metropolitan NSW.     Based on the COVID-19 statistics released on 25 August 2021, NSW Health continued to attempt to determine where each COVID-19 case had been infected, indicating that there had been efforts to contact each COVID-19 case. column103: According to the NSW Government website as of 25 August 2021, masks were mandatory in outdoor public areas and  indoor areas within non-residential premises, as well as on public transport and public transport waiting areas. This policy applied to the whole of NSW, although individuals in LGAs of concern were also specifically required to wear masks in indoor and outdoor areas of markets.    Individuals in NSW were not required to wear a mask when participating in strenuous exercise, undertaking work where clear enunciation or visibility of the mouth was essential, at a correctional facility, place of custody or hospital, working alone in an office, or in the process of getting married.    This was a continuation of existing restrictions. The full list of mask rules and exemptions is available at the following websites:    http://web.archive.org/web/20210825210541/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20210825105153/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area  http://web.archive.org/web/20210825175253/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions  http://web.archive.org/web/20210825213946/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/changes/face-mask-rules
column106: According to the NSW Government website as of 25 August 2021, all individuals aged 18 years and above were allowed to receive a COVID-19 vaccine, and were strongly encouraged to do so. The Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine was the preferred vaccine for 16-59 year olds. The AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine was recommended for those aged 60 years and above, as well as for individuals under 60 years old who could not access the Pfizer vaccine, where the benefits of taking the AstraZeneca vaccine outweighed the risks. As there had been 4,698,473 COVID-19 vaccines administered in NSW as of 12 August 2021 since the beginning of the vaccine rollout, it was plausible that the NSW Government had the capacity to make COVID-19 vaccines available to all.    COVID-19 vaccines for free for everyone in Australia.    This was a continuation of existing policy. column115: According to the NSW Health website as of 28 August 2021, no visitors were allowed in residential aged care facilities except for those providing essential care. All essential care visitors were required to wear a surgical mask, and all visits were to occur in the room of the relevant resident.  Essential visitors were prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities if they had COVID-19 symptoms, were in contact with confirmed COVID-19 cases, or were waiting on the results of a COVID-19 test. Individuals who had visited areas considered to have a high COVID-19 risk (details in the link below) were also prohibited from visited aged care facilities.  Residents of aged care facilities were asked not to leave said aged care facilities unless there was an essential reason to do so.  Due to the lack of archived links, It is unclear whether this was a continuation of existing policy. Nonetheless, directions prohibiting visitors who were likely to have COVID-19 from entering residential aged care facilities had already been in place. This expansion of existing government policy brought the restrictions imposed on all of rural and regional NSW in line with the restrictions placed on Greater Sydney. column15: According to an update made to the NSW Department of Education website on 27 August 2021, stay at home orders would continue to apply to all schools in Greater Sydney until 12:01am on 30 September 2021. All schools in regional NSW were to continue following stay at home orders until 11:59pm on 10 September 2021.    All schools in LGAs of concern (Bayside, Blacktown, Burwood, Campbelltown, Canterbury-Bankstown, Cumberland, Fairfield, Georges River, Liverpool, Parramatta, select suburbs within the Penrith LGA, and Strathfield) were also placed under stay-at-home orders, although it was not specified when these stay at home orders would end.    The update also stated that a staged return to school would begin between 25 October and 8 November 2021 when community vaccination and transmission conditions were met, but no specific regions or LGAs had been identified as having met these criteria.    Year 12 students had been able to return to school in a limited manner when schools faced stay at home orders. As there is a lack of archived webpages detailing the measures year 12 students were required to follow between mid-August and September, the extent to which these students were able to access on-campus facilities is unclear. However, one NSW Department of Education webpage (as of 6 August 2021) stated that year 12 students were only allowed to spend 2 hours at school per day, for a maximum of 5 days per week.    This was an extension of existing stay at home orders announced in regional NSW and LGAs of concern. column79: Tenants who can’t pay their rent in full because they are impacted by the recent COVID-19 outbreak are protected from eviction.  To be eligible for the protection against eviction, a tenant needs to: show that rent paying members of the household are impacted by COVID-19 and have lost employment, work hours or income or have had to stop working because they or other members of their household (or in their care) were/are ill with COVID; and show that the  household’s take home weekly income has reduced by 25% or more (including any government assistance received) compared to the weekly income received in the 4 weeks prior to 26 June 2021; and continue to pay at least 25% of the rent payable.  The 60 day protection against eviction for rental arrears applies to all tenancy agreements, including informal, unwritten agreements.  This is a continuation of existing policy.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210801032604/https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/resource-library/publications/coronavirus-covid-19/property/moratorium

column60: According to the NSW Government website as of 1 September 2021, stay at home restrictions were imposed across NSW. The restrictions in place were largely a continuation of existing policies, and there was some regional variation in State Government policy which did not affect the ordinal coding scale.    In both regional NSW and Greater Sydney, individuals were directed to stay home unless they had a reasonable excuse to leave (e.g. buying groceries, undertaking permitted work that could not be done at home, exercising, or going out for medical and caring reasons). When shopping, exercising, or engaging in outdoor recreation, individuals were required to stay within their LGA or within 5 kilometres of their homes.    Those in LGAs of concern (higher-risk LGAs in Greater Sydney) were required to follow more stringent restrictions in addition to those mentioned above. A curfew was imposed on LGAs of concern between 9pm and 5am (although residents could leave home for approved work and caring reasons, as well as emergencies). Outdoor recreation outside of exercise was not permitted. column24: According to a media release published by NSW Health on 2 September 2021, small wedding services (with no more than 5 guests and a 6-member wedding party) could resume from 3 September 2021. As such, businesses that held weddings services (e.g. pubs, clubs, food and drinks premises, and places of worship) which complied with wedding restrictions were exempt from businesses closure directions.    This was a relaxation of workplace closure restrictions for businesses which hosted small weddings. Other workplace closure restrictions remained the same:    In regional NSW and most of Greater Sydney, most retail premises, entertainment venues and recreational areas, places of worship, and personal care services were required to close.   Businesses which provided essential goods and services were allowed to conduct in-person operations. However, garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores were included in the list of essential businesses which were open to all. The full list of businesses which were allowed to open in Greater Sydney and regional NSW is available at the following websites:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210909032019/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20210908185924/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions    Parts of NSW which were considered to be LGAs of concern (Bayside, Blacktown, Burwood, Campbelltown, Canterbury-Bankstown, Cumberland, Fairfield, Georges River, Liverpool, Parramatta, Strathfield, and parts of Penrith) were required to follow more stringent restrictions. Only businesses which provided essential goods and services were allowed conduct in-person operations. Garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores were only open to relevant tradespeople. Educational and professional development activities were moved online.  The list of businesses which were allowed to operate in LGAs of concern is available at the following websites:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210908121354/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area  http://web.archive.org/web/20210908131454/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules    Other archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210902055232/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/news/Pages/20210902_01.aspx

The NSW Department of Education website also stated that a staged return to school would begin between 25 October and 8 November 2021 when community vaccination and transmission conditions were met, but no specific regions or LGAs had been identified as having met these criteria.    Year 12 students had been able to return to school in a limited manner when schools faced stay at home orders. As there is a lack of archived webpages detailing the measures year 12 students were required to follow between mid-August and September, the extent to which these students were able to access on-campus facilities is unclear. However, one NSW Department of Education webpage (as of 6 August 2021) stated that year 12 students were only allowed to spend 2 hours at school per day, for a maximum of 5 days per week. column106: According to the NSW Government website as of 8 September 2021, all individuals 16 years old and above were eligible for a COVID-19 vaccine. This was a continuation of existing policy.  The Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine was the preferred vaccine for 16-59 year olds. The AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine was recommended for those aged 60 years and above, as well as for individuals under 60 years old who could not access the Pfizer vaccine, where the benefits of taking the AstraZeneca vaccine outweighed the risks. There had been 6,859,279 COVID-19 vaccines administered in NSW as of 31 August 2021 since the beginning of the vaccine rollout, and 89% of individuals aged 16 years old and above had received their first COVID-19 vaccine as of 5 October. As such, it was plausible that the NSW Government had the capacity to make COVID-19 vaccines available to all. COVID-19 vaccines for free for everyone in Australia. column24: According to an announcement made by the NSW Deputy Premier on 9 September 2021, lockdowns in parts of NSW which were considered 'low risk' and had no COVID-19 cases for at least 14 days would be lifted from 12:01am on 11 September 2021. column79: According to the Fair Trading NSW website, the following existing residential tenant protections were in place across NSW until 11 November 2021:     Tenants who couldn't pay their rent in full because they were impacted by COVID-19 outbreak were protected from eviction. To be eligible for the protection against eviction, a tenant needed to:   	- show that rent paying members of the household are impacted by COVID-19 and have lost employment, work hours or income;   	- show that the household’s take home weekly income had decreased by 25% or more (including any government assistance received) compared to the weekly income received in the 4 weeks prior to 26 June 2021; and   	- continue to pay at least 25% of the rent payable. column115: According to NSW Health, the screening advice for residential aged care facilities and home care service providers has been updated for 13 September 2021.     The key messages for this update include:   1. Some areas of NSW (in parts of regional NSW) are currently no longer under stay at home Orders. Residents in facilities not under stay at home Orders may have two visitors per day provided they do not come from a stay at home area (parts of regional NSW, Greater Sydney, and areas of concern within Greater Sydney).     2. Aged care residents in facilities under stay at home Orders are permitted to leave the facility to exercise (go for a walk) provided they:   - remain within 1km of the facility   - do not interact with other people outside of the facility   - wear a facemask or carry a medical certificate or other written evidence signed by a registered health practitioner or a statutory declaration by the person saying they have a physical or mental health illness or condition which prohibits them from wearing a facemask   - are risk assessed by the facility that they are capable of undertaking exercise in a COVID safe way.       3. Aged care residents in facilities not under stay at home Orders:   - Are permitted to leave the facility and attend small family gatherings but must abide by the current COVID-19 Safety gathering and movement restrictions   - Must not go into an area that is currently under a stay at home Order.
