Individuals in LGAs of concern within Greater Sydney had to follow additional restrictions - they were required to register to work outside their own LGA, and could only exercise and buy groceries within 5km of their homes.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210916172025/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions  https://web.archive.org/web/20210917032528/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20210916200412/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area  https://web.archive.org/web/20210916053650/https:/www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/border-restrictions    Individuals arriving in NSW from the ACT, Queensland, and Victoria were required to complete a travel declaration. Exemptions were in place for residents of some border communities.  Close contacts who had been to areas of high concern in these states were prohibited from entering NSW if they were not NSW residents. Those allowed to enter were required to self-isolate for 14 days.  Casual contacts who had been to areas of high concern in these states required a negative COVID-19 test result to enter if they were not NSW residents. Those already in NSW were required to self-isolate for 14 days or until they received a negative COVID-19 test result.    Those who had been to areas of concern in the ACT and Victoria were required to refrain from leaving home without a reasonable excuse for 14 days.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220714092333/https://www.pmc.gov.au/sites/default/files/publications/covid-19-restrictions-tracker-2021-09-16.pdf
column74: As published on Department of Home Affairs website, Australia’s borders are currently closed and entry to Australia remains strictly controlled to help prevent the spread of COVID-19. Travel to Australia is only available if you are exempt or you have been granted an individual exemption.  This represents continuation in the COVID-19 policy response.   https://web.archive.org/web/20211007004301/https://covid19.homeaffairs.gov.au/travel-restrictions
column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418. - The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments  https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment
column103: There were regional variations in NSW mask mandate policies, which were a continuation of existing policies.    According to a NSW Health article published on 16 Sep 2021, masks remained mandatory for all indoor public venues in low-risk regional NSW LGAs, including public transport, front-of-house hospitality, retail and business premises, on planes and at airports. Only hospitality staff were required to wear a mask when outdoors. Children aged under 12 did not need to wear a mask.     For other areas in the state (Greater Sydney, some regional NSW LGAs under stay at home restrictions, and LGAs of concern), according to the Public Health (COVID-19 Additional Restrictions for Delta Outbreak) Order (No 2) 2021 [NSW], the mandatory mask rule still applies with exceptions - masks were mandatory in all indoor and outdoor areas outside the home, although individuals were not required to wear masks when working alone indoors.    More information is available in the following clauses of the Order:   	- For general areas: see clauses 2.7-2.9;   	- For stay-at-home areas: see clauses 3.15-3.17;   	- For areas of concern: see clauses 4.16-4.18  	  Archived link: https://web.archive.org/web/20211130041202/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/news/Pages/20210916_02.aspx   https://web.archive.org/web/20211006060024/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20(COVID-19%20Additional%20Restrictions%20for%20Delta%20Outbreak)%20Order%20(No%202)%202021_210916.pdf

column79: According to the Fair Trading NSW website (as of 23 September 2021) the following existing residential tenant protections were in place across NSW until 11 November 2021:     Tenants who couldn't pay their rent in full because they were impacted by COVID-19 outbreak were protected from eviction. To be eligible for protection against eviction, a tenant needed to:   	- show that rent paying members of the household are impacted by COVID-19 and have lost employment, work hours or income;   	- show that the household’s take home weekly income has reduced by 25% or more (including any government assistance received) compared to the weekly income received in the 4 weeks prior to 26 June 2021; and   	- continue to pay at least 25% of the rent payable.     In addition to this, some landlords with tenants affected by COVID-19 were also eligible for a COVID-19 land tax benefit of a Residential Tenancy Support Payment of up to $3000 per tenancy.    This is a continuation of existing policy.   Archived links: https://web.archive.org/web/20210813210201/https://www.service.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/financial-support-individuals-and-households https://web.archive.org/web/20210923114457/https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/resource-library/publications/coronavirus-covid-19/property/moratorium

column15: According to an update made to the NSW Department of Education website on 20 September 2021, the NSW Government continued to maintain a targeted policy regarding learning from home.    Students in high-risk LGAs of concern (located within Greater Sydney) were to undertake learning from home, and there would be minimal staff onsite to support students who were unable to learn from home. A similar policy applied to parts of Regional NSW where stay at home orders for school were still in place. Learning from home would also continue in Greater Sydney until 30 September 2021.    Students in some low-risk regional LGAs were allowed to return to school in a COVID-safe manner, with masks required for all staff and students in Year 7 and above*.     Students in Year 12 and those completing their HSC exams in 2021 had already been able to undertake a limited return to school. Due to a lack of archived material, it is unclear what directions were imposed on Year 12 students on 20 September 2021, but they may have been given special timetables to limit mingling between students according to the NSW Department of Education website (as last updated on 2 October 2021).    The NSW Department of Education website maintained that a staged return to school would begin between 25 October and 8 November 2021 when community vaccination and transmission conditions were met, but it was unclear whether any specific LGAs met this criteria.    *The full list of LGAs where in-person learning was permitted is available in the below websites. This was subject to relatively frequent changes as the risk of COVID-19 transmission changed over time in different LGAs. column69: There were some regional variations in State Government policy, but this did not trigger changes in the ordinal scale.    According to a media release by the NSW Premier Gladys Berejiklian and the NSW Minister for Health and Medical Research Brad Hazzard, individuals in LGAs of concern (high-risk areas in Greater Sydney) could exercise or go grocery shopping 5km from their homes OR anywhere within their LGA. This was a relaxation of existing policies in LGAs of concern, and came into effect at 12:01am on 20 September 2021.  http://web.archive.org/web/20211129214305/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/restrictions-to-ease-lgas-of-concern    According to the NSW Government website as of 20-22 September 2021, other internal movement restrictions remained the same:    Individuals in the regional LGAs not under stay at home restrictions* were unable to travel to stay at home LGAs in NSW without a reasonable excuse to do so.  *Note: regional LGAs were often moved in and out of stay at home restrictions. See the archived link for details.  http://web.archive.org/web/20210922214841/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/limited-restrictions    Individuals in parts of NSW under stay at home restrictions (parts of regional NSW, Greater Sydney, and LGAs of concern) could only exercise and go grocery shopping within their LGA or 5km from their home if possible. Those living in Greater Sydney (including in LGAs of concern) needed to register to travel more than 50km from Greater Sydney for work. Individuals in LGAs of concern within Greater Sydney had to follow additional restrictions - they were required to register to work outside their own LGA.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210920191650/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  https://web.archive.org/web/20210920194117/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions  http://web.archive.org/web/20210920194523/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area  https://web.archive.org/web/20220714124007/https://www.pmc.gov.au/sites/default/files/publications/covid-19-restrictions-tracker-2021-09-23.pdf    Individuals arriving in NSW from the ACT, Queensland, and Victoria were required to complete a travel declaration. Those allowed to enter were required to self-isolate for 14 days.  Casual contacts who had been to areas of high concern in these states required a negative COVID-19 test result to enter if they were not NSW residents. Those already in NSW were required to self-isolate until they received a negative COVID-19 test result. column42: There were some minor regional variations in NSW Government policy, but these generally did not trigger changes in the ordinal coding scale:    According to an announcement made on 21 September 2021 on the NSW Health website, children aged 18 years old in parts of NSW under stay at home orders would be allowed to create 'friends bubbles' from noon on 21 September 2021. This was a relaxation of existing restrictions.   A friends bubble was a group of three friends who could visit each other's homes for play and activity. Friends bubbles were subject to the following conditions:  	- Everyone in a friends bubble had to live in the same LGA or within 5 kilometres of each other  	- Everyone aged 18+ in each participating household was required to be fully vaccinated or have a medical exemption  	- Parents and carers dropping their children off at friends' houses were not allowed to interact with other parents  	- The members of a friends bubble must stay the same, and each child could only be part of one friends bubble.    Other gathering restrictions remained the same:    In parts of NSW under stay at home orders (some regional LGAs, Greater Sydney, and LGAs of concern), up to 5 fully vaccinated or 2 unvaccinated individuals aged 16 years old or above could gather together for outdoor recreation. Individuals were not permitted to accept visitors (other than nominated visitors or people in their friends bubble) unless there was an essential reason to do so (e.g. for necessary childcare arrangements, permitted work, or compassionate reasons).    In some regional NSW LGAs which were no longer under stay at home orders, up to 5 visitors were allowed in a home regardless of vaccination status. The maximum number of people permitted at outdoor events was as follows:  	a) For major recreation outdoor facilities - 5000 people  	b) For controlled outdoor public gatherings - 500 people  	c) For COVID-19 safe outdoor public gatherings - 50 people  	d) For all other outdoor gatherings - 20 people.  Note that regional NSW LGAs were often moved in and out of stay and home restrictions. See the archived links for more information and the status of different LGAs. column60: Many regional LGAs in lockdown with low case transmission rate were moved out of stay at home requirements on 11/09/2021, however, after increased transmission were recognised some of these regional LGAs moved back into lockdown, and out, for different periods of time until 11/10/2021. The restrictions include not being able to leave the house except for essential reasons This represents a loosening of policy for some of the state but a continuation for some regional locales and Greater Sydney.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220202095840/https://www.nsw.gov.au/media-releases/lockdown-lifted-parts-of-regional-nsw  See this link for regional LGA under stay at home orders as of 22/09/2021 https://web.archive.org/web/20210922041136/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions
column106: The following directions were a continuation of existing policies.    According to vaccine rollout statistics from 22 September 2021, the NSW Health website, and a press conference conducted by the Federal Minister for Health and Aged Care and the Deputy Chief Medical Officer on 12 September 2021, vaccines were available for individuals aged 12 years old and above. As of 22 September 2021, 31.51% of 12-15 year olds* and 84.11% of those aged 16 years and above in NSW had received the first dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, indicating that the universal availability policy could be met.    Although it is unclear which vaccine brands 12-15 year olds had access to in NSW between 22 September and 3 October 2021 (due to a lack of archived links), the aforementioned press conference stated that those aged 12 years and above could access the Pfizer and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines. The NSW Government website stated that the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine was mainly administered to those aged 60 years old and above.    COVID-19 vaccines continued to be free for everyone in Australia.     *12-15 year olds  became eligible for COVID-19 vaccines on 13 September 2021. column115: According to NSW Health, there were no changes to existing aged care policies*. There were regional variations in policy which triggered changes in the ordinal scale.    Aged care residents in facilities not under stay at home Orders (i.e. facilities in some low-risk regional NSW LGAs):   	- Were permitted to leave the facility and attend small family gatherings as long as they could abide by the current COVID-19 Safety gathering and movement restrictions   	- Were not permitted to go into an area currently under a stay at home Order.  	- Were permitted to have up to 2 visitors per day as long as the visitors did not come from a stay at home area    Aged care residents in facilities under stay at home Orders (i.e. facilities in some parts of regional NSW LGAs, Greater Sydney, and areas of concern in Greater Sydney) were permitted to leave the facility to exercise (go for a walk) provided they:   	-  remained within 1km of the facility   	- did not interact with other people outside of the facility   	- wore a facemask or carried a medical certificate or other written evidence signed by a registered health practitioner or a statutory declaration by the person saying they had a physical or mental health illness or condition which prevented them from wearing a facemask   	- had received approval to exercise in a COVID safe way.     	  Other restrictions applied across NSW:  No visitors were allowed in residential aged care facilities except for those providing essential care. All essential care visitors were required to wear a surgical mask, and all visits were to occur in the room of the relevant resident. Essential visitors were prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities if they had COVID-19 symptoms, were in contact with confirmed COVID-19 cases, or were waiting on the results of a COVID-19 test. Individuals who had visited areas considered to have a high COVID-19 risk (details in the link below) were also prohibited from visited aged care facilities.     *aside from additional staff vaccination requirements, which came into effect on 17 September 2021 and are not recorded in this indicator    Archived links  https://web.archive.org/web/20210916043909/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/racf-latest-advice.aspx  https://web.archive.org/web/20211106001855/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/information/covid19-legislation

column90: The following contact tracing initiatives were a continuation of existing policies. There was some regional variation in policy but this did not trigger a change in the ordinal coding scale.    According to the NSW Government website as of 22 September 2021, NSW Health conducted contact tracing interviews and investigations to determine whether confirmed COVID-19 cases presented a public health risk at the venues they visited. This information was used to publish contact locations and/or notify people who were likely to be exposed to COVID-19.    In metropolitan Sydney, contact tracing efforts focused on higher-risk areas  where transmission was deemed likely to occur. NSW Health identified all contact locations in areas outside metropolitan Sydney (including casual contact venues with a very low risk of transmission).     Based on the COVID-19 statistics released on 22 September 2021, NSW Health continued to attempt to determine where each COVID-19 case had been infected, indicating that there had been efforts to contact each COVID-19 case.  Businesses were also required to keep records of people entering their premises to assist with these efforts. column103: According to the Public Health (COVID-19 Additional Restrictions for Delta Outbreak) Order (No 2) 2021 (as in force from 3:03pm on 23 September 2021) individuals in low-risk regional LGAs which were not under stay at home restrictions who had been to stay at home areas in NSW in the past 14 days were required to wear masks in all outdoor areas outside from home and all indoor common areas in residential premises in addition to the other locations where they were already required to wear a mask. This was a tightening of existing restrictions, and came into effect from 3:03pm on 23 September 2021.    All other mask requirements remained the same:    In low-risk regional NSW LGAs which were not under stay at home orders, individuals were required to wear masks in all indoor areas outside of home. Hospitality staff were required to wear masks outdoors.  In stay at home areas (Greater Sydney, some regional NSW LGAs under stay at home restrictions, and LGAs of concern), masks were mandatory in all indoor and outdoor areas outside of home, as well as in indoor common areas in residential premises.    Across NSW, masks were not required for children under 12 or when working alone indoors. A full list of exceptions to the mask mandate is available in the archived links.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211006090947/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20(COVID-19%20Additional%20Restrictions%20for%20Delta%20Outbreak)%20Order%20(No%202)%202021_210923_3.03pm.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20220324052429/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/information/covid19-legislation/temporary-movement-gathering-restrictions

column24: There were no significant policy changes which would trigger changes in the ordinal coding scale. There were regional variations in State Government policy.    According to the NSW Government website as of 22 September 2021, and amendments to the Public Health (COVID-19 Additional Restrictions for Delta Outbreak) Order (No 2) 2021 made on 23 and 24 September 2021, some parts of regional NSW which were considered low-risk did not have stay-at-home restrictions in place. Retail stores, hospitality venues, personal care services, recreational and sporting facilities, as well as entertainment venues could open subject to a 1 person per 4 square metre rule indoors. Gyms were required to follow capacity limits for group classes.  Note that some regional LGAs were frequently moved in and out of stay at home restrictions. The full list of low-risk regional LGAs and the restrictions they were required to follow can be found at the following links:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210922214841/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/limited-restrictions  https://web.archive.org/web/20211006055346/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20(COVID-19%20Additional%20Restrictions%20for%20Delta%20Outbreak)%20Order%20(No%202)%20Amendment%20(No%2016)%20Order%202021.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20211123100256/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20%28COVID-19%20Additional%20Restrictions%20for%20Delta%20Outbreak%29%20Order%20%28No%202%29%202021_210911.pdf       Other LGAs in regional NSW and most of Greater Sydney continued to follow stay at home restrictions. Under these restrictions, most venues were required to close.   Businesses which provided essential goods and services were allowed to conduct in-person operations. Garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores were included in the list of essential businesses which were open to all. The full list of businesses which were allowed to open in Greater Sydney and parts of regional NSW affected by COVID-19 is available at the following websites:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210925065138/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney   http://web.archive.org/web/20210924015326/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions       Parts of NSW (more specifically, Greater Sydney) which were considered to be LGAs of concern (Bayside, Blacktown, Burwood, Campbelltown, Canterbury-Bankstown, Cumberland, Fairfield, Georges River, Liverpool, Parramatta, Strathfield, and parts of Penrith) were required to follow more stringent restrictions. Only businesses which provided essential goods and services were allowed conduct in-person operations. Garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores were only open to relevant tradespeople.  http://web.archive.org/web/20210924160129/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area
column33: There were no significant policy changes which would trigger changes in the ordinal scale. There were regional variations in State Government policy.    According to the NSW Government website as of 22 and 27 September 2021, some low-risk regional LGAs which were not under stay at home restrictions* could continue to hold public events. Major recreation outdoor facilities (such as theme parks and stadiums) could reopen with 1 person per 4 square metres or up to 5000 people. Controlled outdoor public gatherings (i.e. smaller ticketed and seated events) could reopen with up to 500 people attending. COVID-Safe outdoor gatherings could proceed with a maximum of 50 people attending. All other public outdoor gatherings could proceed with a maximum of 20 people attending.  Hospitality and entertainment venues could open with density restrictions in place.  *Note that regional LGAs were often moved in and out of stay at home restrictions. No more than two unvaccinated people or 5 vaccinated people from different households were allowed to gather unless they had an essential or permitted reason to do so (e.g. they were undertaking permitted work, legal, or educational activities that could not be conducted remotely, or they were attending a permitted wedding or funeral service with no more than 10-11 people). Nonessential venues continued to be closed.  http://web.archive.org/web/20210924015326/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions   http://web.archive.org/web/20210925065138/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20210924160129/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area
column60: The following restrictions were generally a continuation of existing restrictions - there were no policy changes which triggered changes in the ordinal coding scale.    According to the NSW Government website as of 22 and 27 September 2021, some regional NSW LGAs which were considered low-risk were not required to follow stay at home restrictions. column74: Australian borders are closed except for those who have an exemption. column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418. - The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments
column79: The following State Government policies applied to the whole of NSW:    According to a media release published on the NSW Government website on 2 September 2021, the NSW Government announced an increase to the Residential Tenancy Support Package. This would allow some landlords who offered rent reductions to tenants affected by COVID-19 to claim up to $4500 per tenancy.   Several online sources (including the Fair Trading NSW website and the Ethnic Communities' Council of NSW), indicate that the online application for the $4,500 payment was available from 24 September 2021. This was a strengthening of contract relief policy - prior to 24 September 2021, eligible landlords could only claim up to $3000 per tenancy.    Other rent relief policies remained the same:  According to the Fair Trading NSW website (as of 23 September 2021), tenants who couldn't pay their rent in full because they were impacted by COVID-19 outbreak were protected from eviction. To be eligible for protection against eviction, a tenant needed to:  	-  show that rent paying members of the household are impacted by COVID-19 and have lost employment, work hours or income;   	- show that the household’s take home weekly income has decreased by 25% or more (including any government assistance received) compared to the weekly income received in the 4 weeks prior to 26 June 2021; and   	- continue to pay at least 25% of the rent payable. column15: According to the NSW Department of Education website, students in parts of NSW which were subject to stay at home orders (Greater Sydney, LGAs of concern, and some parts of regional NSW) were required to learn from home as part of Level 4 restrictions which were in place. Some limited exemptions were granted to Year 12 students (who could attend school for a maximum of 3 hours a day and were subject to other directions to prevent unnecessary mingling) and students who were unable to learn from home.  Some schools (located in low-risk localities within regional NSW) were operating at Level 3 ( COVID-safe: further restrictions on activities and non-essential visitors) where they opened with COVID-Safe measures such as mask-wearing in place. column24: Although worker capacity restrictions on outdoor renovation sites across NSW were lifted on 27 September 2021*, there were no significant changes to workplace closure policies which would trigger changes in the ordinal coding scale.    According to the NSW Government website as of 29 October 2021 and 2 October 2021, some parts of regional NSW which were considered to be low-risk (see archived link for more details) were not required to follow stay at home orders. Retail stores, hospitality venues, personal care services, recreational and sporting facilities, as well as entertainment venues could continue to open subject to a 1 person per 4 square metre rule indoors. Gyms were required to follow capacity limits for group classes.  Note that the list of low-risk regional LGAs changed frequently as outbreaks began and ended in different parts of NSW.  http://web.archive.org/web/20210929013625/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/limited-restrictions   http://web.archive.org/web/20211002194555/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/limited-restrictions     According to the NSW Government website as of 1 October 2021, parts of regional NSW which were affected by COVID-19 as well as Greater Sydney were required to follow stay at home orders. Under these restrictions, most venues were required to close.   Businesses which provided essential goods and services were allowed to conduct in-person operations. Garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores were included in the list of essential businesses which were open to all. The full list of businesses which were allowed to open in Greater Sydney and parts of regional NSW affected by COVID-19 is available at the following websites:  http://web.archive.org/web/20211001142906/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20211001152834/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions    According to the NSW Government website as of 1 October 2021, higher risk LGAs of concern (which were located in Greater Sydney) continued to follow stay at home orders. However, the list of businesses which were allowed to open to the general public was expanded to include garden centres, plant nurseries, hardware stores, landscaping supply stores, agricultural supply stores, and pet supply stores. This was a relaxation of existing restrictions in LGAs of concern, although it is unclear when this was implemented due to a lack of archived material.  http://web.archive.org/web/20211001185824/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area    *see   http://web.archive.org/web/20211001222542/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/authorised-workers/renovations-repairs-maintenance-and-cleaning#local-government-areas-of-concern
column33: There were no significant policy updates that would trigger a change in the ordinal coding scale. There were regional variations in State Government policy. Major recreation outdoor facilities (such as theme parks and stadiums) could reopen with 1 person per 4 square metres or up to 5000 people. Controlled outdoor public gatherings (i.e. smaller ticketed and seated events) could reopen with up to 500 people attending. COVID-Safe outdoor gatherings could proceed with a maximum of 50 people attending. All other public outdoor gatherings could proceed with a maximum of 20 people attending.  Hospitality and entertainment venues could open with density restrictions in place.  *Note that regional LGAs were often moved in and out of stay at home restrictions. See the archived link for more details.  http://web.archive.org/web/20211002194555/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/limited-restrictions    According to the NSW Government website as of 24 and 25 September 2021, areas under stay at home restrictions (some regional LGAs, Greater Sydney, and LGAs of concern) continued to cancel public events. No more than two unvaccinated people or 5 vaccinated people from different households were allowed to gather unless they had an essential or permitted reason to do so (e.g. they were undertaking permitted work, legal, or educational activities that could not be conducted remotely, or they were attending a permitted wedding or funeral service with no more than 10-11 people). Nonessential venues continued to be closed.  http://web.archive.org/web/20211001152834/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions  http://web.archive.org/web/20211001142906/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20211001142910/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area    Note: from 11 October onwards the NSW Government would implement differentiated restrictions for vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals attending different venues.  http://web.archive.org/web/20211010034256/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/limited-restrictions  http://web.archive.org/web/20211010113121/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/greater-sydney  http://web.archive.org/web/20211010190406/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-regions  http://web.archive.org/web/20211010171626/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/affected-area

column69: According to the NSW Health website as of 1-2 October 2021, there were some regional variations in State Government policy, but this did not trigger changes in the ordinal scale. The following policies were generally a continuation of existing policies.    Individuals in the regional LGAs not under stay at home restrictions* were unable to travel to stay at home LGAs in NSW without a reasonable excuse to do so.  *Note: regional LGAs were often moved in and out of stay at home restrictions. See the archived link for details.  http://web.archive.org/web/20211002194555/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/limited-restrictions    Individuals in parts of NSW under stay at home restrictions (parts of regional NSW, Greater Sydney, and LGAs of concern) could only exercise and go grocery shopping within their LGA or 5km from their home if possible. Those travelling to Greater Sydney were only allowed to do so with a reasonable excuse, and were required to stay home for 14 days after returning unless there was a reasonable excuse to do so.  Those living in Greater Sydney (including in LGAs of concern) needed to register to travel more than 50km from Greater Sydney for work. Individuals in LGAs of concern within Greater Sydney had to obtain a permit and undergo COVID-19 testing to work outside their LGA.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211001171159/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/public-health-orders.aspx#gathering    Individuals arriving in NSW from the ACT, Queensland, and Victoria were required to complete a travel declaration. Exemptions were in place for residents of some border communities.  Close contacts who had been to areas of high concern in these states were prohibited from entering NSW if they were not NSW residents. Those allowed to enter were required to self-isolate for 14 days.  Casual contacts who had been to areas of high concern in these states required a negative COVID-19 test result to enter if they were not NSW residents. Those already in NSW were required to self-isolate until they received a negative COVID-19 test result.    Those who had been to areas of concern in the ACT and Victoria were required to refrain from leaving home without a reasonable excuse for 14 days.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211002013840/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/rules/interstate-hotspots

column77: -	People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 7 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments.
column79: The following regulations were a continuation of existing policies and applied to the whole of NSW:    According to the Fair Trading NSW website as of 6 October 2021, residential tenancy support packages were available for eligible tenants and landlords affected by COVID-19.    As part of these packages, tenants who couldn't pay their rent in full because they were impacted by COVID-19 outbreak were protected from eviction. To be eligible for protection against eviction, a tenant needed to:  	-  show that rent paying members of the household are impacted by COVID-19 and have lost employment, work hours or income;   	- show that the household’s take home weekly income had decreased by 25% or more (including any government assistance received) compared to the weekly income received in the 4 weeks prior to 26 June 2021; and   	- continue to pay at least 25% of the rent payable.     In addition to this, some landlords with tenants affected by COVID-19 were also eligible for a COVID-19 land tax benefit of a Residential Tenancy Support Payment of up to $4500 per tenancy.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211006091648/https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/resource-library/publications/coronavirus-covid-19/property/moratorium

column90: The following contact tracing initiatives were a continuation of existing policies. There was some regional variation in policy but this did not trigger a change in the ordinal coding scale.    According to the NSW Government website as of 1 October 2021, NSW Health conducted contact tracing interviews and investigations to determine whether confirmed COVID-19 cases presented a public health risk at the venues they visited. This was used to create a webpage with case locations and alerts to inform the public about locations where they may have been exposed to COVID-19. Some people who came into contact with COVID-19 cases were also contacted directly by NSW Health.    In metropolitan Sydney, contact tracing efforts focused on higher-risk areas where transmission was deemed likely to occur. NSW Health identified all contact locations in areas outside metropolitan Sydney (including casual contact venues with a very low risk of transmission).     Based on the COVID-19 statistics released on 30 September 2021, NSW Health continued to attempt to determine where each COVID-19 case had been infected, indicating that there had been efforts to contact each COVID-19 case.     https://web.archive.org/web/20211001071149/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/case-locations-and-alerts.aspx   https://web.archive.org/web/20210930073852/https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/covid-19/Pages/stats-nsw.aspx
column103: The following restrictions were a continuation of existing policy. There were some regional variations in State Government policy.    According to the Public Health (COVID-19 Additional Restrictions for Delta Outbreak) Order (No 2) 2021 (as in force from 1 October 2021), individuals in some low-risk regional NSW LGAs ("the general area") were required to wear a mask in all indoor areas outside of the home. Hospitality staff were required to wear a mask outdoors when interacting with members of the public.     Individuals in stay at home areas (Greater Sydney and parts of regional NSW) and areas of concern, as well as those who had visited these areas in the past 14 days were required to wear masks in all indoor and outdoor areas outside of home, as well as indoor common areas in residential premises. column106: According to vaccine rollout statistics from 01 October 2021, the NSW Health website, and a press conference conducted by the Federal Minister for Health and Aged Care and the Deputy Chief Medical Officer on 12 September 2021, vaccines were available for anyone aged 12 years old and above. The vaccine brands which were administered were AstraZeneca (mainly for those aged 60 years old and above), Pfizer and Moderna (for those aged 12 years old and above).  COVID-19 vaccines continues to be free for everyone in Australia. column115: According to NSW Health, there were no changes to existing aged care policies. There were regional variations in policy which triggered changes in the ordinal scale.    Aged care residents in facilities not under stay at home Orders (i.e. facilities in some low-risk regional NSW LGAs):   	- Were permitted to leave the facility and attend small family gatherings as long as they could abide by the current COVID-19 Safety gathering and movement restrictions   	- Were not permitted to go into an area currently under a stay at home Order.  	- Were permitted to have up to 2 visitors per day as long as the visitors did not come from a stay at home area    Aged care residents in facilities under stay at home Orders (i.e. facilities in some parts of regional NSW LGAs, Greater Sydney, and areas of concern in Greater Sydney) were permitted to leave the facility to exercise (go for a walk) provided they:   	-  remained within 1km of the facility   	- did not interact with people outside of the facility   	- wore a mask or carried a medical certificate or other written evidence signed by a registered health practitioner or a statutory declaration by the person saying they had a physical or mental health illness or condition which prevented them from wearing a facemask   	- had received approval to exercise in a COVID safe way.     	  Other restrictions applied across NSW:  No visitors were allowed in residential aged care facilities except for those providing essential care. column77: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. column69: According to the NSW Government website (as of 26 November and 6 December 2021), the NSW Health website (as of 28 November 2021), and the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice (as approved on 12 and 27 November 2021), the following restrictions were largely a continuation of existing restrictions and applied to the whole of NSW. Some locations in the ACT, Queensland, and Victoria were listed as places of high concern, and individuals who had visited these places were required to follow travel restrictions when entering NSW:    Close contacts of COVID-19 cases who had been to places of high concern interstate (as listed in the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice) and were not NSW residents were prohibited from entering NSW if they were not fully vaccinated. Vaccinated close contacts entering NSW were required to self-isolate until it had been at least 7 days after they had last visited a place of high concern. column69: According to the NSW Government website (as of 13 December 2021), the NSW Health website (as of 9 and 15 December 2021), and the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice (as approved on 13 December 2021) the following restrictions were largely a continuation of existing restrictions and applied to the whole of NSW, although some restrictions placed on unvaccinated individuals were lifted on 15 December 2021.    Unvaccinated individuals in NSW were prohibited from going on holidays or recreation outside their LGA. All unvaccinated residents of Victoria above the age of 16 were prohibited from travelling to NSW for holiday or recreation purposes.  According to the Public Health (COVID-19 General) Order (No 2) 2021, which came into effect on 15 December 2021, these restrictions were lifted on 15 December 2021.    Vaccinated individuals did not face any restrictions on travel within NSW.    Some locations in the ACT, Queensland, and Victoria were listed as places of high concern, and individuals who had visited these places were required to follow travel restrictions when entering NSW:    Close contacts of COVID-19 cases who had been to places of high concern interstate (as listed in the NSW COVID-19 Concerns Notice) and were not NSW residents were prohibited from entering NSW if they were not fully vaccinated. Vaccinated close contacts entering NSW were required to self-isolate until it had been at least 7 days after they had last visited a place of high concern. column90: According to the NSW Government website as of 6 and 16 December 2021, although the NSW Government is no longer publishing a list of venues visited by COVID-19 cases, "NSW Health will continue to contact people diagnosed with COVID-19 and their close contacts." Businesses may need to undertake a risk assessment and assist NSW Health in providing specific advice to clients, customers or patrons. NSW Health will especially focus contact tracing on:   - household members of cases   - contacts among family and friends of cases   - places where there are people at high risk of severe disease such as in healthcare, aged care, disability care and correctional facilities   - places transmission has been identified   - places that provide essential services such as schools and food distribution facilities. column115: The following restrictions were largely a continuation of existing policy, which applied to the whole of NSW. column115: The following restrictions were largely a continuation of existing policy, which applied to the whole of NSW. column51: As of 12 April 2021, public transport, including buses, taxis and rideshare services, continues to operate in the Northern Territory (NT). To minimise the risk of contracting or spreading coronavirus (COVID-19), passengers must practice good hygiene and physical distancing where possible. This includes sitting in the back seat of vehicles when using ridesharing or taxi services. Public transport is essential at this stage but will be reviewed regularly. Non-essential travel is to be avoided. This represents a continuation of policy response to Covid-19.    Advice to drivers of public transport includes: drivers of point to point vehicles should carry out good hygiene practices to protect themselves and passengers from the spread of illness.  You do not need to wear a mask if you are healthy and more information can be found in the following web archive link below.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210223182535/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/travel/public-transport

column74: Between 14 April and 21 April, "Australia’s borders are closed. column15: Greater Darwin entered into lockdown for another 72 hours from 28 June 2021 according to Chief Health Officer Dr Hugh Heggie. This lockdown policy has extended from part of Greater Darwin (announced on the 27 June 2021) to the whole Greater Darwin Area. All people in Greater Darwin are required to stay in their home or accommodation during the lockdown. There are only be five reasons to leave home. These include:    -To receive health care or attend medical appointments. Including to get the COVID-19 vaccine.  -To undertake shopping and get necessary goods and services. column77: Individuals may be eligible for various types of income support. There are three main types. column79: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. These Notices provide the framework for the Territory’s response to tenancy issues arising as a result of the COVID-19 emergency.    The amendments increased the notice timeframes for Termination other than breaches of agreement to 60 days for both fixed term and periodic tenancy agreements (currently 14 days for fixed term agreements and 42 days for periodic tenancies). It also extended the length of time that rent has to be in arrears for termination for non-payment of rent where COVID 19 hardship is present to 60 days (originally 14 days of rent arrears). Unpaid rent is still owed to landlords.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211104045430/https://consumeraffairs.nt.gov.au/rental-changes-due-to-covid-19/overview-of-modifications-to-processes

column79: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. column79: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. These Notices provide the framework for the Territory’s response to tenancy issues arising as a result of the COVID-19 emergency. The amendments increased the notice timeframes for Termination other than breaches of agreement to 60 days for both fixed term and periodic tenancy agreements (currently 14 days for fixed term agreements and 42 days for periodic tenancies). It also extended the length of time that rent has to be in arrears for termination for non-payment of rent where COVID 19 hardship is present to 60 days (originally 14 days of rent arrears). column60: Following the end of the lockdown in Darwin and Katherine, residents of these areas could leave home for any reason (see post-lockdown announcement: https://web.archive.org/web/20220101053023/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/updates/items/2021-08-19-lockdown,-restrictions-and-border-entry-requirements). column103: Immediately following the lockdown in Darwin and Katherine, people over 12 years old must wear masks in public places (outside homes and private vehicles) whenever they cannot maintain a 1.5-m distance from others, or when their job requires them to work within 1.5 m of others (e.g. waiters, hairdressers, beauty therapists).   Exceptions for people who:  -	cannot wear a mask because of a medical condition  -	are engaged in vigorous exercise  -	need to communicate with a hearing-impaired person  -	must remove their mask to verify their identity  -	must remove their mask to receive medical treatment  -	remove their mask for the purpose of teaching at school or child care  -	must remove their mask in an emergency.  See post-lockdown directions at https://web.archive.org/web/20220201233900/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/1037825/cho-directions-no45-2021.pdf.

column79: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418. - The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments  https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment

column15: From 5 November 2021, Greater Darwin entered a lockout for three days. column24: On November 8, the NT government announced that the lockout for Greater Darwin will extend for a further 24 hours, until 11.59pm Tuesday 9 November 2021.  Katherine exited lockout from 5pm today. From this time, there will be no restrictions in Katherine on the reasons to leave home for people who are vaccinated and unvaccinated, but mask wearing will remain in place to reduce the risk of COVID-19 in the community. For one hour of outdoor exercise a day within 5 km from your home with one other person or people from your house. column79: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. These Notices provide the framework for the Territory’s response to tenancy issues arising as a result of the COVID-19 emergency.    The amendments increased the notice timeframes for Termination other than breaches of agreement to 60 days for both fixed term and periodic tenancy agreements (currently 14 days for fixed term agreements and 42 days for periodic tenancies). It also extended the length of time that rent has to be in arrears for termination for non-payment of rent where COVID 19 hardship is present to 60 days (originally 14 days of rent arrears). Unpaid rent is still owed to landlords.  This policy remained current on 30 November 2021.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211104045430/https://consumeraffairs.nt.gov.au/rental-changes-due-to-covid-19/overview-of-modifications-to-processes

A mask mandate will remain in place in Greater Darwin and Katherine regions until 5pm on Friday 12 November 2021.    		- If you are in Greater Darwin or Katherine, a mask mandate will be in place until 5:00pm on Friday 12 November.  		These restrictions include:  		· Face masks must be worn outside of the home when you are unable to maintain a physical distance of 1.5 metres – this includes at places like the supermarket, shops, the hairdresser and on public transport. Workers who come into close contact with patrons, or who work in crowded environments will need to wear a mask. You do not have to wear a mask while exercising or playing sport.  		· Patrons at restaurants, cafes and pubs must wear a mask unless eating or drinking. Dance floors can open but masks must be worn.  		· Travel will be permitted across the Territory but restrictions continue to apply and follow you, if you travel outside the lockout area.    This represents an easing of COVID restrictions in Darwin.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220230845/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/updates/items/20221-11-9-covid-19-update-lockout-to-end-for-darwin.-one-new-positive-case-recorded

column24: According to the business guidelines and safety plans posted on the Northern Territory government on 2 July 2021, all businesses in the Northern Territory can operate normally but are required to lodge a COVID-19 Safety plans. column15: On November 15, 2021, 	the Security and Emergency Management Committee (SEMC) this afternoon made the decision under the Northern Territory (NT) pandemic plan to lockdown parts of the NT following two positive cases of COVID-19. Effective from 6:00pm, the Municipality of Katherine including Tindal and Robinson River including the surrounding homelands will enter into lockdown for 72 hours.    Lockdown details for Katherine and Robinson River and surrounding homelands:  From 6:00pm, residents must stay at home for the lockdown period and people are only permitted to leave for the following five reasons:  			1. Medical treatment, including COVID testing or vaccination  			2. For essential goods and services, like groceries and medications. For Robinson River residents, only one household member should visit the store, once per day.  			3. For work that is considered essential  			4. For one hour of outdoor exercise a day within 5 km from your home with one other person or people from your house  			5. To provide care and support to a family member or person who cannot support themselves. In case of an emergency.    Schools and childcare centres will be open only for the children of essential workers. Schools and early childhood services in Robinson River and the surrounding homelands will be closed.    This represents a tightening of COVID restrictions in these areas.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220233824/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/updates/items/2021-11-15-positive-cases-in-the-nt,-lockdowns-in-katherine,-robinson-river-and-surrounds

column15: According to the NT government website, parts of the territory entered a snap lockdown on Nov 15th 2021 which would force schools to close. Schools were only open to children of essential workers, and it was not clear on the exact measures universities in these regions were taking, however, it is assumed they were also closed due to the lockdown. Only schools in the Katherine and Robinson River regions were closed, the rest of the territory was unaffected.     This represented a strengthening of school closure policy for the affected regions, and a continuation of policy of regions not impact by the lockdown.    The lockdown was set to end on Nov 22nd 2021, which would be when schools were presumably opened back up.    Funding for parents of children affected:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220217004423/https://www.dese.gov.au/covid-19/announcements/covid19-northern-territory-extra-support-child-care-katherine-lockdown-extended    Announcement:   https://web.archive.org/web/20220217004521/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/updates/items/2021-11-15-positive-cases-in-the-nt,-lockdowns-in-katherine,-robinson-river-and-surrounds

column79: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. column79: On 28 April 2020 and 11 May 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed COVID-19 Modification Notices and amendments that impact the processes involved in the Residential Tenancies Act 1999. column69: The following travel restrictions are in place in the Northern Territory;  Double vaccinated visitors are welcome to enter the Northern Territory without having to quarantine. Only Therapeutic Goods Administration approved COVID-19 vaccines are accepted for the purpose of travel to Australia and the Northern Territory and proof of vaccination will be required on arrival.  Children aged 15 years and under are considered to be vaccinated for the purposes of entry into the NT only.  Unvaccinated returning Territorians and those people who have received authority to enter the Northern Territory, will be required to undertake 14 days mandatory supervised quarantine at their own cost.  Unvaccinated visitors are not permitted to enter the NT.  For vaccinated travellers;  •	You must have a negative COVID-19 PCR test up to three days before you arrive in the NT and must be able to show proof of the result on arrival.  •	You are required to have a COVID-19 Rapid Antigen Test test (RAT) within three days after arriving in the NT and another test on Day 6 after arriving in the NT. You are not required to isolate after these tests.  Additionally, there are a number of exclusion zones within the Northern Territory which restrict travel within the Territory;  •	You cannot travel to an excluded community unless you are a resident of that community or an essential worker for the purpose of work.  •	To enter you must have a negative Rapid Antigen Test the day of travel and before you enter community.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211229123720/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/travel/border-entry  https://web.archive.org/web/20220114020411/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/travel/exclusion-zones

column115: The Northern Territory Chief Health Officer has implemented a number of restrictions on Aged Care Facilities including entry and collection of information requirements for visitors and workers along with required Covid-19 procedures for aged care facilities. column24: Between the 30th December and the 5th January there was a continuation of the existing policy enacted by the Northern Territory Government, requiring mandatory vaccination of workers in key areas. Workers who were likely to come into contact with vulnerable peoples, in high risk Covid-19 settings or who perform work in essential infrastructure, food, or essential goods security or supply or logistics in the Northern Territory were all subject to mandatory vaccination requirements.   Based on these restrictions, workplace closing is coded to 2G for unvaccinated workers. For vaccinated workers, this would be coded to 0 during this period. column33: Between the 30th December and the 5th January, the NT Government did not require or recommend any cancellation of events. column103: Masks were mandatory at all major NT airports and while onboard an aircraft during this time. These were the only mandatory mask restrictions in the Northern Territory during this time. column106: As announced by the Australian Government department of health on Mar 22nd 2021, phase 1b of the Australian national vaccine rollout was due to start on April 1st 2021. column115: According to the Queensland legislative registrar, current aged care policy had been in place since March 13th 2021. column42: According to the Queensland legislative registrar, restrictions regarding gatherings had been superseded at 12pm on April 15th 2021. Significant amendments now allowed for gatherings of 500 people (indoors) without submitting a COVID-Safe event plan, instead having to only apply hygiene measures for the attendees. Venues (e.g. restaurants) were also allowed to operate at a 1 person per 4 square metre rule. No cap on the capacity was indicated. This policy was applied to the whole of QLD.     This represents an easing of restrictions for the whole of QLD. The restrictions that were in place were superseded on this date as a result of no emerging cases following the previous outbreak.    This policy was in place for the whole of the following time period. No significant amendments were indicated until late June 2021. column33: As of 1 September 2021, there is no new policy regarding cancel public events for vaccinated/non-vaccinated visitors to public events in Queensland, however, there are restrictions on how individuals can enter public events:    Indoor events:  Events at indoor spaces must operate in accordance with a COVID Safe Event Checklist which includes the following requirements:  - a maximum occupant density of 1 person per 2m2 or 100% allocated seated and ticketed capacity  - collection of contact tracing information using the Check In Qld app  - regular and thorough cleaning  - availability of hand washing facilities or hand sanitiser.    Events with patron dancing:  Indoor or outdoor events with patron dancing must operate in accordance with a COVID Safe Event Checklist. The checklist includes the following additional requirements for events with patron dancing:  - operate an area for dancing on the basis that no more than 1 person per 2m2 dances in the dance area  - implement control measures to manage crowding in dance areas.    Outdoor events without patron dancing:  Outdoor events without patron dancing do not need to operate in accordance with a COVID Safe Event Checklist, however the following requirements still apply:  - appropriate public health controls including cleaning, hygiene measures, regular washing of hands and availability of hand sanitiser  - people at the event observe physical distancing to the extent possible.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210808033049/https://www.covid19.qld.gov.au/government-actions/covid-safe-events

column33: As of 15 September 2021, there is no new policy regarding cancel public events for vaccinated/non-vaccinated visitors to public events in Queensland, however, there are restrictions on how individuals can enter public events:    Indoor events:  Events at indoor spaces must operate in accordance with a COVID Safe Event Checklist which includes the following requirements:  - a maximum occupant density of 1 person per 2m2 or 100% allocated seated and ticketed capacity  - collection of contact tracing information using the Check In Qld app  - regular and thorough cleaning  - availability of hand washing facilities or hand sanitiser.    Events with patron dancing:  Indoor or outdoor events with patron dancing must operate in accordance with a COVID Safe Event Checklist. column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418. - The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments  https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment

column77: -	People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 7 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments.

column69: Restrictions on interstate movement are in place. In Summary, the Queensland government distinguishes between border regions (restricted vs non-restricted) and 'Covid-19' Hotspots. The policies outlined below are a continuation of policies prior to 15 November 2021.    Queensland residents and residents of the non-restricted border zone area that have entered the NSW restricted border areas can enter Queensland for 'limited essential purposes'. The full list of limited essential purposes can be found in [3]. Movement between the border regions must have a Queensland entry pass.    Fully vaccinated domestic travellers arriving in Queensland by air from a COVID-19 hotspot at the Brisbane airport may be eligible to quarantine at their home or another nominated private residence in Queensland.    Anyone else who has been to a COVID-19 hotspot in the last 14 days or since their start date identified for the hotspot (whichever is shorter) will not be allowed to enter Queensland unless they are a Queensland resident, someone relocating to Queensland (i.e. a new resident) or have an exemption. Anyone allowed to enter will need to complete 14 days mandatory quarantine. Effective immediately, on 27/November/2021, anyone who is not a citizen or permanent resident of Australia, or their immediate family including parents of citizens, and who have been in African countries where the Omicron variant has been detected and spread – within the past 14 days – will not be able to enter Australia. column69: The Border Restrictions Direction (No.58), which was effective between 13 December 2021 and 30 December 2021, stated that individuals who had been to a listed COVID-19 hotspot (NSW, ACT, VIC, Greater Adelaide, and parts of NT) in the past 14 days could not travel to Queensland unless they met the following criteria:     - They had been fully vaccinated  - They had received a negative COVID-19 test from the COVID-19 hotspot within 72 hours of arriving in Queensland  - If remaining in Queensland on the fifth day after arrival, they were required to get tested for COVID-19 as close to the fifth day after arrival as possible.  - They were not an international arrival    Unvaccinated border zone residents (from NSW LGAs on the border with Queensland) who had been to a restricted border zone LGA (Moree Plains Shire, except for Tulloona, Garah, Boomi, Mungindi, Toomelah and Boggabilla) without entering any other COVID-19 hotspots in the past 14 days were only allowed to travel to Queensland for essential purposes. They were only allowed to stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to fulfill the essential purposes. These residents were required to follow home quarantine directions if staying overnight or longer.    Fully vaccinated border zone residents who had been to a restricted border zone LGA without entering any other COVID-19 hotspots in the past 14 days were only allowed to travel to Queensland for limited purposes. They were only allowed to stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to fulfill the limited purposes.    Unvaccinated border zone residents who had not been to a restricted LGA or a COVID-19 hotspot in the past 14 days could only enter to for a permitted purpose, and could only stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to complete the permitted purpose.    Fully vaccinated border zone residents who had not been to a restricted LGA or a COVID-19 hotspot in the past 14 days could enter Queensland with no further restrictions.    Individuals who had been to an interstate exposure location, or were identified as close, casual, or secondary contacts of a COVID-19 case, and had to fulfill isolation requirements in another Australian State or Territory were not permitted to enter Queensland, regardless of whether or not they had fulfilled any other requirements necessary to enter Queensland.    This was a continuation of existing COVID-19 restrictions. column90: The Queensland Government did not state whether it was conducting contact tracing for all cases of COVID-19 on its contact tracing webpage between 22-28 December 2021.  It only stated that Queenslanders could fill out a form to notify authorities if they had visited any listed close contact exposure locations, and fulfill testing and quarantine requirements if they had visited casual or low risk contact locations. Queensland Health also contacted affected business and households not listed on its webpage. Another Queensland Government webpage (as of 29 December 2021) stated that authorities would contact positive COVID-19 cases to identify contacts, although it is unclear whether this was being done for every single case.  Although businesses and activities were required to collect contact information from staff and visitors for contact tracing during this period of time, some local news reports suggested that this was not always feasible, and that extensive contact tracing was not always conducted. According to a news article published in the Brisbane Times on 22 December 2021, the Chief Health Officer of Queensland reportedly stated that "as the [COVID-19 case] numbers increase, the amount of investigation that the public health units will do will reduce" in regards to local contact tracing.    Considering that Queensland recorded 189 new cases on 22 December 2021, and this number increased steadily to 1,158 new cases on 28 December 2021, it is likely that the Queensland Government was unable to conduct comprehensive contact tracing for every single positive COVID-19 case during this time period.    Official Queensland Government statements (published on Government websites between 22-28 December 2021) regarding the comprehensiveness of contact tracing were a continuation of existing messaging. However, since the daily COVID-19 case numbers were much higher during this time period than they were in the month prior (with 6 new cases recorded on 6 December 2021, and 0 new cases recorded on 22 November 2021), it is likely that contact tracing became less comprehensive at some point during, or directly prior to 22-28 December. column106: According to the Queensland Government website (as of 2 November 2021 and 4 January 2022), COVID-19 vaccines were free for all Australian citizens, permanent residents, and most visa holders. All individuals aged 12 and over were able to receive the Pfizer (Comirnaty) or Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine, and adults aged 60 years and above could receive the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) vaccine. The AstraZeneca vaccine could be taken by those under 60 years old if they had already received a dose of the AstraZeneca vaccine without serious side effects, and had made an informed decision to take the vaccine, where the benefits of taking it outweighed the risks.    It is likely that vaccines were able to be administered to the vast majority of the eligible Queensland population, since 85% of Queenslanders had already been fully vaccinated as of 22 December 2021.    COVID-19 booster shots were also available for Queenslanders over 18 who had received their second dose of a COVID-19 vaccine more than 5 months ago. The Pfizer (Comirnaty) and Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccines were the recommended vaccines for booster shots, although the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) vaccine was available for individuals who could not take the Pfizer or Moderna vaccines and had already taken 2 doses of the AstraZeneca vaccine previously.    The directions in place between 22-28 December 2021 were a continuation of existing vaccine policy. Aged care residents with COVID-19 (if possible) and visitors were directed to wear a surgical mask.  Residential aged care facilities were also directed to follow standard hygiene, cleaning, and disinfection protocol, as well as additional national infection control standards (such as restricting visitor and staff movement, refraining from admitting new residents during COVID-19 outbreaks, and protocols for handling residents to minimise the risk of COVID-19 transmission)  *Due to the broad range of exceptions allowing unvaccinated visitors to enter residential aged care facilities, H8 was coded as 2G for both vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals. The directions in place between 22-23 December 2021 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policy restrictions.
