column69: According to the Queensland Government website, interstate arrivals who had been to a COVID-19 hotspot  (NSW, ACT, VIC, Greater Adelaide, and parts of NT) in the past 14 days were no longer required to take a COVID-19 test on the 5th day after arrival unless they had COVID-19 symptoms or were a close contact of a person with COVID-19. This represented a relaxation of existing COVID-19 border restrictions.    Interstate travellers were still required to follow all other relevant directions in the Border Restrictions Direction (No.58), which was effective between 13 December 2021 and 30 December 2021. This stated that hotspot travellers could not visited Queensland unless they had met the following criteria:    - They had been fully vaccinated  - They had received a negative COVID-19 test from the COVID-19 hotspot within 72 hours of arriving in Queensland  - They were not an international arrival    Unvaccinated border zone residents (from NSW LGAs on the border with Queensland) who had been to a restricted border zone LGA (Moree Plains Shire, except for Tulloona, Garah, Boomi, Mungindi, Toomelah and Boggabilla) without entering any other COVID-19 hotspots in the past 14 days were only allowed to travel to Queensland for essential purposes. They were only allowed to stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to fulfill the essential purposes. These residents were required to follow home quarantine directions if staying overnight or longer.    Fully vaccinated border zone residents who had been to a restricted border zone LGA without entering any other COVID-19 hotspots in the past 14 days were only allowed to travel to Queensland for limited purposes. They were only allowed to stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to fulfill the limited purposes.    Unvaccinated border zone residents who had not been to a restricted LGA or a COVID-19 hotspot in the past 14 days could only enter to for a permitted purpose, and could only stay in Queensland for the duration of time necessary to complete the permitted purpose.    Fully vaccinated border zone residents who had not been to a restricted LGA or a COVID-19 hotspot in the past 14 days could enter Queensland with no further restrictions.    Individuals who had been to an interstate exposure location, or were identified as close, casual, or secondary contacts of a COVID-19 case, and had to fulfill isolation requirements in another Australian State or Territory were not permitted to enter Queensland, regardless of whether or not they had fulfilled any other requirements necessary to enter Queensland. column90: According to the Queensland Government (updated on 31 December 2021), from 31 December 2021, they will only notify of major outbreak venues or super-spreader events in Queensland. They are no longer routinely listing exposure sites in Queensland since transmission of COVID-19 is now widespread throughout metropolitan, regional and remote Queensland. People need to consider any movement through the Queensland community as a risk for COVID-19 infection. This indicates a stricter standard of listing exposure sites as the number of exposure sites and the frequency of listing exposure sites are reduced.    According to the Queensland Government’s Twitter post on December 2021, from 31 December 2021, Queensland is adopting a nationally-agreed definition of a COVID-19 close contact and isolation periods for people who have tested positive. Under the new definition, a diagnosed person is someone who has tested positive to COVID-19, either through a PCR or a rapid antigen test (RAT).    You are a close contact if you are a household member or a household-like contact of a diagnosed person:  -	A household member is a person who ordinarily resides at the same premises or place of accommodation as the diagnosed person, and who are residing at the premises or place of accommodation at the time the diagnosed person receives their positive COVID-19 test result. You do not have to be related to the diagnosed person to be considered a household member.  -	A household-like contact is a person who has spent more than four hours with the diagnosed person in a house or other place of accommodation, care facility or similar.  Note: a person is not a household-like contact if they are in a separate part of the house, accommodation or care facility that has a separate point of entry and no shared common areas, and if they do not have contact or interaction for more than four hours.    This means that unless your workers are living in the same household as a confirmed covid case, they will not be considered close contacts and will not have to get tested (unless they have symptoms).    This indicates a stricter standard of contact tracing as the scope of contacts is narrower.    Although the Check In App is still in operation, the size of contact tracing is smaller. It shall be considered as less comprehensive than before.    Therefore, it should be reported as 1. column69: The SA Government commenced a number of state border restrictions on 31 January 2021 and these continue on 1 February 2021. Anyone who has been in Western Australia in the previous 14 days was not permitted to enter South Australia. Anyone who arrived in SA from WA on or after 26 January must immediately self-quarantine for 14 days, commencing 31 January. COVID-19 tests are required immediately and again on day 5 and day 12 of quarantine. column77: No new policy measures.   On 21 April 2020, the South Australian Government announced a new $13.8 million support package for South Australia’s international education sector. The funding, which is part of the Community and Jobs Support Fund, is designed to support international students residing in South Australia impacted by the coronavirus restrictions.  The International Student Support Package will include:  •	$10 million fund for university students significantly impacted by COVID-19 restrictions at the University of Adelaide, Flinders University and University of South Australia to distribute to their pathway and international students  •	a $500 emergency cash grant to other international students significantly impacted by the restrictions, currently enrolled in a course, living in South Australia and who meet the criteria  •	a one-off $200 assistance payment per student living with South Australian families provided to homestay families. There is also the South Australian COVID-19 Cluster Isolation Payment which is a single $300 payment to provide financial support to workers in SA who are required to self-isolate because of a public health direction from SA Health and mandatory COVID-19 testing, and do not have access to paid leave or other income support. column79: State Parliament has endorsed a number of initiatives aimed at helping landlords and tenants whose incomes have been affected by COVID-19. For tenants, the emergency measures acknowledge the inability for tenants to be able to fulfil their financial responsibilities to landlords as a result of circumstances beyond their control.  Measures to protect tenants include:  •	Ensuring tenants cannot be evicted by landlords due to an inability to paid rent because of COVID-19 employment loss  •	Preventing landlords from increasing rent during the COVID-19 period  •	Ensuring that COVID-19 is a designated form of undue hardship for matters being heard by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) where disputes arise.  Importantly, the legislation does not specify what, if any, rent reduction should occur. The government encourages tenants to carefully consider their need to use the above measures. If a tenant has been affected by COVID-19 but can still pay their rent, they are encouraged to continue doing so. The International Student Support Package will include:  •	$10 million fund for university students significantly impacted by COVID-19 restrictions at the University of Adelaide, Flinders University and University of South Australia to distribute to their pathway and international students  •	a $500 emergency cash grant to other international students significantly impacted by the restrictions, currently enrolled in a course, living in South Australia and who meet the criteria  •	a one-off $200 assistance payment per student living with South Australian families provided to homestay families.  Archived link: https://web.archive.org/web/20210224141152/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/school-and-community/schools-universities-and-childcare   There is also the Australian government’s pandemic leave payment available to people in SA, up to $1500 for eligible people who have been instructed by an SA health official to self-isolate or self-quarantine at home because they have covid-19 or been in close contact with a confirmed case, or care for a child 16 years and under who has covid-19 or been in close contact with a confirmed case.   People may also be eligible if they are at lest 17 years old living in SA, have a right o work in Australia but unable to go to work and earn an income and have no appropriate leave entitlements.  There is also the South Australian COVID-19 Cluster Isolation Payment which is a single $300 payment to provide financial support to workers in SA who are required to self-isolate because of a public health direction from SA Health and mandatory COVID-19 testing, and do not have access to paid leave or other income support. Archived link: http://web.archive.org/web/20210524003649/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/school-and-community/financial-support-for-individuals  See also https://web.archive.org/web/20210227110158/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/pandemic-leave-disaster-payment-south-australia
column79: State Parliament has endorsed a number of initiatives aimed at helping landlords and tenants whose incomes have been affected by COVID-19.  For tenants, the emergency measures acknowledge the inability for tenants to be able to fulfil their financial responsibilities to landlords as a result of circumstances beyond their control.  Measures to protect tenants include:  •	Ensuring tenants cannot be evicted by landlords due to an inability to paid rent because of COVID-19 employment loss  •	Preventing landlords from increasing rent during the COVID-19 period  •	Ensuring that COVID-19 is a designated form of undue hardship for matters being heard by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) where disputes arise.  Importantly, the legislation does not specify what, if any, rent reduction should occur. The government encourages tenants to carefully consider their need to use the above measures. If a tenant has been affected by COVID-19 but can still pay their rent, they are encouraged to continue doing so. Archived link: https://web.archive.org/web/20210224140104/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/school-and-community/housing-and-in-the-community

column69: Effective 12.01am 26 February 2021, people are permitted to enter South Australia from Victoria. There are no testing or quarantine requirements.  People currently in quarantine from Greater Melbourne are no longer required to complete the 14 day quarantine period, provided they did not visit a ‘Tier 1’ exposure site identified on the Victorian Department of Health and Human Services website. column79: In South Australia, state parliament has endorsed a number of initiatives aimed at helping landlords and tenants whose incomes have been affected. These measures, which are still in place on 1 April 2021, apply to residential tenancies, rooming houses and residential parks. These initiatives are expected to be in place until 31 September 2021, or 28 days after all relevant declarations relating to COVID-19 have ceased - whichever comes first. Previously these measures were due to cease on 31 May 2021 or 28 days after all relevant declarations have ceased.  These measures aim to: institute a short-term moratorium on eviction for non-payment of rent due to severe rental distress as a result of COVID-19, prevent landlords from increasing rent, where the tenant is suffering financial hardship due to COVID-19, extend the tenant’s ability to arrange to have repairs carried out by agreement with the landlord and provide a general protection for tenants who breach their agreement as a result of complying with a direction under law relating to COVID-19.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210626024003/https://www.cbs.sa.gov.au/rental-advice-due-covid-19

column79: In South Australia, state parliament has endorsed a number of initiatives aimed at helping landlords and tenants whose incomes have been affected. column115: On 10 April 2020, the State Coordinator made a Direction under the Emergency Management Act 2004 to limit entry into residential aged care facilities and this Direction is in effect on 22 May 2021. The Emergency Management (Residential Aged Care Facilities No 36) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 states that a person is prohibited from entering a residential aged care facility unless they are in certain categories including: resident, employee, providing goods or services, providing care and support. People must not enter under a range of circumstances including: during the last 14 days have arrived in South Australia from an interstate location that is not a low community transmission zone, is unwell with a fever or respiratory symptoms or is awaiting results from a COVID-19 test. Broadly, this Direction has not changed significantly from version to version. The main change is to reflect the interstate cases and the related restrictions on people visiting from those areas.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210815035954/https://legislation.sa.gov.au/web/information/CV19/EMA-CEASED/Emergency%20Management%20%28Residential%20Aged%20Care%20Facilities%20No%2036%29%28COVID-19%29%20Direction%202021_21.05.2021_CEASED.pdf

column69: The Emergency Management (Cross Border Travel-Associated Direction No 12) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 took effect on 24 May 2021. column33: Public events are continuing to take place in South Australia on 29 May 2021. column79: In South Australia, state parliament has endorsed a number of initiatives aimed at helping landlords and tenants whose incomes have been affected. These measures, which are still in place on 29 May 2021, apply to residential tenancies, rooming houses and residential parks. These initiatives are expected to be in place until 31 September 2021, or 28 days after all relevant declarations relating to COVID-19 have ceased - whichever comes first. Previously these measures were due to cease on 31 May 2021 or 28 days after all relevant declarations have ceased.  These measures aim to: institute a short-term moratorium on eviction for non-payment of rent due to severe rental distress as a result of COVID-19, prevent landlords from increasing rent, where the tenant is suffering financial hardship due to COVID-19, extend the tenant’s ability to arrange to have repairs carried out by agreement with the landlord and provide a general protection for tenants who breach their agreement as a result of complying with a direction under law relating to COVID-19.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210801112436/https://www.cbs.sa.gov.au/rental-advice-due-covid-19

column79: The South Australian state parliament has endorsed a number of initiatives aimed at helping landlords and tenants whose incomes have been affected. column77: -	People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 7 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments.
column79: The emergency measures acknowledge the inability for tenants to be able to fulfill their financial responsibilities to landlords as a result of circumstances beyond their control.  Measures to protect tenants include:  •	Ensuring tenants cannot be evicted by landlords due to an inability to pay rent because of COVID-19 employment loss  •	Preventing landlords from increasing rent during the COVID-19 period  •	Ensuring that COVID-19 is a designated form of undue hardship for matters being heard by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) where disputes arise.  •	Landlords who provide tenants impacted by COVID-19 with rent relief may be eligible for a 25% reduction on the land tax payable on a parcel of land in the 2019-20 land tax year.  •	Relief is also available to residential and non-residential landowners who are unable to secure a tenant because of COVID-19. To be eligible for land tax relief, eligible landlords will need to demonstrate that the land was leased to 30 March 2020, but has since been vacant due to the impact of COVID-19.    These measures have been endorsed by the State Parliament and apply to residential tenancies, rooming houses, and residential parks. They are expected to remain in place until 1st December 2021, or 28 days after all relevant declarations relating to COVID-19 have ceased - whichever comes first.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211003061351/https://www.covid-19.sa.gov.au/school-and-community/housing-and-in-the-community

column77: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. column115: According to The Emergency Management (Residential Aged Care Facilities No 43) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 which was implemented from 12:31 pm on 24 November 2021, individuals were prohibited from entering a residential aged care facility unless they were residents of the facility, worked at the facility (as an employee, contractor, student, or volunteer), were conducting a prospective resident visit, were providing essential goods or services (including legal, medical, emergency management, or regulatory services) for the facility or its residents, were conducting a care or support visit for a resident at the facility, or were participating in a group activity led by a worker from the facility.    The above individuals were prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities if they had COVID-19 symptoms, had contact with a known COVID-19 case without wearing PPE in the 14 days preceding entry, had not received the influenza vaccine since 1 June 2021 (unless they were observing the waiting period between the COVID-19 and influenza vaccines), were awaiting a COVID-19 test result (unless their COVID-19 test was for the purpose of routine monitoring of asymptomatic individuals), or were prohibited from entering due to an Arrivals direction (e.g. they had been in a high-risk area in the 14 days prior to entry). Masks were mandatory for workers and visitors in residential aged care facilities when in the presence of other persons.    The Emergency Management (Residential Aged Care Facilities No 43) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 also specified different regulations for care and support visits according to aged care facility vaccination rates. Residents of aged care facilities with a vaccination rate of less than 70% were only allowed to receive two care and support visits with one person OR one care and support visit with two people per day. Residents of aged care facilities with a vaccination rate of more than 70%, as well as residents receiving end of life support were not subjected to these visitor restrictions.    In addition to the new Direction, the 24 November 2021 version of the SA Government website stated that individuals could only enter aged care facilities if they had received all doses of an approved COVID-19 vaccine.  COVID-19 vaccines were highly recommended for aged care facility residents.    Aged care workers were only allowed to provide personal care at one residential aged care facility (if possible), and were not allowed to work at their aged care facility if they had worked in a medi-hotel in the past 14 days. They also had to complete COVID-19 training modules and wear PPE. All aged care facilities were required to submit workforce management and infection control plans.      The directions introduced on 24 November 2021 represented a tightening of previous COVID-19 restrictions to limit entry into aged care facilities, and the directions in place between 25 November 2021 and 2 December 2021 were a continuation of these restrictions. Due to the presence of vaccine-related restrictions H8 was coded as 3G, although it would be coded as 2G if allowances for vaccinated visitors and staff were taken into account. For instance, some South Australian universities such as the University of Adelaide and the University of South Australia expected students to wear masks whilst indoors and encourage social distancing. This followed SA Health directions as of 22 October 2021, which strongly recommended mask wearing in adult educational institutions.  The University of South Australia also moved some of its services online as of 22 November 2021. column24: According to the 19 November 2021 version of the Current Activity Restrictions webpage on the SA Government website, there were no mandates requiring the closure of workplaces (except for shisha bars).    However, businesses were required to implement COVID-safe measures such as 1.5m social distancing and density restrictions (3/4 density for seated activities, 1/2 density for non-seated activities, 1/4 density for indoor fitness facilities), as well as the use of an approved contact tracing system. Employers were also required to ensure that their businesses had 'adequate and accessible facilities' to enable workers to practice good hand hygiene.    In addition to these measures, many workplaces also followed industry-specific COVID-safe practices. These included (but were not limited to) mandatory mask-wearing in high-risk settings (such as in aged care and disability facilities, some healthcare facilities, correctional facilities, and Aboriginal communities) and personal care settings, vaccination and PPE requirements in aged care facilities, the provision of flexible working arrangements in the public service, and cleaning requirements in hospitality venues.    Residential aged care facility workers, police workers, most healthcare workers, point to point drivers working from Adelaide, Mount Gambier, Parafield or Port Lincoln Airports, workers within the SA quarantine system, and some commercial transport workers were required to have received at least 1 dose of a TGA-approved vaccine in order to attend work. For this reason C2 was coded as 2G, even though a 1G code would apply to vaccinated workers.    This represents a continuation of existing COVID-19 policy, although mask-wearing was no longer required in schools from 25 November 2021 and vaccination requirements for point to point drivers at select South Australian airports came into effect on 25 November 2021. column33: According to the SA Government webpages describing COVID-19 restrictions for businesses and COVID management plans, public events with large numbers of attendees were required to either have a COVID-safe plan, a COVID Management Plan, or both.  A COVID Management Plan was a comprehensive plan detailing specific measures to reduce the risk of COVID-19 transmission between attendees and staff. Defined public activities and activities with more than 100 attendees were also required to utilise approved contact tracing systems.    In general, venues with no drinking and dancing, or venues with drinking and dancing attended by fewer than 1000 patrons were required to submit COVID-Safe plans, as were defined public activities with 100-1000 people attending.  A defined public activity included activities where food or beverages were to be consumed, sport and recreation activities, public assemblies and indoor public meetings, the provision of personal care and public entertainment, the operation of nightclubs and licensed premises, the operation of casinos and gaming areas, property auctions and inspections, driver instruction, as well as the provision of healthcare, residential care, disability support and aged care.    All activities, events, and gatherings attended by more than 1000 people, as well as licensed premises providing entertainment of a sexually explicit nature were required to have a COVID Management Plan. Activities, events, or gatherings with over 1000 attendees and multiple vendors were required to submit both a COVID Management Plan (for the event as a whole) and COVID-Safe plans (for individual vendors).    The directions in place between 25 November 2021 and 2 December 2021 represented a continuation of existing COVID-19 policy. column69: According to the SA Government EntryCheck webpage (as of 25 November 2021), all unvaccinated individuals were prohibited from entering the state unless they had successfully applied for an exemption. All individuals (regardless of vaccination status) travelling to SA from interstate or overseas was required to apply to do so through EntryCheck SA    Arrivals from 'very low risk' Australian jurisdictions with no evidence of COVID-19 community transmissions could enter South Australia if they were vaccinated.    Arrivals from 'low risk' Australian jurisdictions with evidence of COVID-19 community transmissions and a vaccination rate of 90% or higher (e.g. the ACT, NSW, and Victoria) were required to take a COVID-19 test within 72 hours prior to arrival in SA as well as complete a daily COVID-19 symptom check for 14 days after arrival.    Arrivals from 'moderate risk' Australian jurisdictions with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a vaccination rate of 80% or higher were required to do the following:  	- Take a COVID-19 test within 72 hours before arriving in SA, as well as within 24 hours after arrival in SA  	- Quarantine in SA until they had taken a COVID-19 test  	- Complete a daily COVID-19 symptom check for 14 days after arrival    Arrivals from 'high risk' Australian jurisdictions with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a full dose vaccination rate of 80% or lower were required to do the following:  	- Obtain a negative COVID-19 test result in the 72 hours prior to arrival in SA  	- Quarantine for 7 days  	- Complete a COVID-19 test 24 hours, 6 days, and 13 days after arrival in SA  	- Complete a daily COVID-19 symptom check for 14 days after arrival  	- Refrain from entering high risk settings and COVID Management Plan events for 14 days after arrival    From the SA Government website as of 25 November 2021, fully vaccinated individuals from cross-border communities and unvaccinated cross-border community members aged between 12 years and 2 months and 18 years could apply to enter SA.  Cross-border community members were required to have a COVID-19 test within 24 hours of their arrival in SA if they had left the cross-border corridor on the NSW or Victorian side for more than 72 hours.  Cross-border communities included those within the NSW Cross Border Corridor (which was comprised of the City of Broken Hill LGA, Unincorporated Far West NSW, and Wentworth) and the Victorian Cross Border Corridor (which was comprised of the Glenelg Shire Council, Hindmarsh Shire Council, Horsham Rural City Council, Mildura Rural City Council, Southern Grampians Shire Council, and the West Wimmera Council)    This represented a continuation of existing restrictions. column77: According to the 6 September 2021 and 29 November 2021 versions of the SA Government website, eligible individuals who were part of a designated COVID-19 cluster and were required to self-isolate whilst waiting for a COVID-19 test result were able to receive a single lump sum payment of $300 dollars from the SA Government.    Individuals could only receive the $300 payment if they:  	- Had visited a COVID-19 exposure site in SA from 21 August 2021 onwards,  	- Had undertaken a COVID-19 test  	- Were required to self-isolate pending the test result and were also scheduled to work during this time  	- Had no access to paid leave or income support  	- Were at least 17 years old and an Australian citizen or permanent resident, or a holder of necessary visa and work permits    Eligible South Australians could also access the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment if they were unable to earn an income whilst self-isolating or caring for someone with COVID-19, but this was an initiative of  the Federal Government.    These support measures were a continuation of existing COVID-19 directions. column79: According to the SA Government's Housing and Community Support webpage (as of 17 November 2021) and the Attorney-General's Department, the State Parliament endorsed the following emergency measures to assist landlords and tenants whose incomes had been affected by COVID-19:  	- Tenants were unable to be evicted by landlords as a result of an inability to pay rent due to COVID-19 employment loss  	- Landlords would be unable to increase rent (if tenants were unable to afford a rent increase)  	- Tenants would have more power to arrange for repairs to be carried out by agreement with their landlords  	- COVID-19 was established as a form of undue hardship, where matters relating to COVID-19 could be resolved by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT). Landlords whose tenants were damaging property and/or opportunistically using COVID-19 to avoid recourse were able to hold these tenants accountable for their actions through SACAT.  	- Landlords providing tenants impacted by COVID-19 with rent relief may have been eligible to receive a 25% reduction in land tax for a parcel of land payable in the year 2019-2020  	- Landlords may have also been eligible for land tax relief if their land was leased to 30 March 2020 but had since been vacant due to COVID-19.    The above measures were expected to be in place until 1 December 2021 or 28 days after all relevant declarations relating to COVID-19 have ceased, whichever came first.    The SA Government's Care and Support webpage also stated that individuals with low or fixed incomes may be eligible for concessions or payments to assist with various living expenses, but these appeared to be existing income support measures unrelated to COVID-19.    Overall, the debt and contract relief measures represented a continuation of existing measures. column90: The SA Government did not explicitly state whether it had been conducting contact tracing efforts for all COVID-19 cases. However, it continued to update its exposure site webpage, which contained a comprehensive list of sites which COVID-19 cases had visited and the public may have been exposed to the virus. In addition to this, retail premises, businesses conducting a defined public activity, activities with more than 100 attendees, private functions, and passenger transport services were required to utilise an approved contact tracing system, enabling SA Health to identify and contact those who may have been exposed to COVID-19. Individuals who tested positive for COVID-19 were also contacted directly by public health officials to identify close contacts.    Considering this information, and the fact that there were less than 5 new COVID-19 cases per day in SA between 25 November 2021 and 1 December 2021 (although there were 19 new cases identified on 2 December 2021), it is likely that the SA Government conducted contact tracing for at least the vast majority of COVID-19 cases. column69: SA state gov C7 (interstate arrivals) 2G 26/11  According to the SA Police website, the new Emergency Management (Arrivals Associated No 2) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 came into effect at 4:56 pm on 26 November 2021. This led to the following changes in interstate border restrictions:    - Close contacts of COVID-19 cases diagnosed in the 7 days prior to arrival in SA were prohibited from entering the state.  - Close contacts of COVID-19 cases diagnosed in the 14 days prior to arrival in SA were required to take a COVID-19 test on the 13th day after exposure, as well as any other COVID-19 test required on their entry approval.  - Domestic violence arrivals (regardless of vaccination status) were allowed to enter SA but were subject to quarantine requirements depending on their circumstances.  - Cross Border Community members who had left their respective corridors for more than 72 hours or travelled to an LGA outside their Corridor were subject to additional testing and quarantine requirements depending on the risk level of the location they had travelled to  - Cross Border Community members travelling into SA with children younger than 12 years and 2 months were required to have a negative pre-arrival COVID-19 test and daily symptom checks for 14 days after arrival.  - Arrivals from Nhill were also subject to COVID-19 testing requirements upon or prior to arrival.    These changes represented a tightening of existing border control measures. Previous interstate travel requirements which were not covered by the changes (see C7 note for 25 November 2021) continued to apply. According to the SA Police website, the new Emergency Management (Arrivals Associated No 3) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 came into effect at 5 pm on 27 November 2021. This led to the following changes to interstate border restrictions:    	- In response to the emergence of the Omicron Variant, individuals arriving from High Risk locations in Australia were required to undertake 14 days of quarantine as well as fulfill pre- and post-arrival testing requirements, daily symptom checks, and venue entry restrictions specified in the directions for 25 November 2021  	- Travellers from low or moderate risk LGAs were required to show evidence of a negative COVID-19 test result within 72 hours before arrival  	- NSW Cross Border Community members were no longer required to complete a daily symptoms check    Most of these changes reflected a tightening of existing border control measures. Previous interstate requirements which were not covered by the changes (see C7 notes for 25 and 26 November 2021) continued to apply. column115: According to the Emergency Management (In-home and Community Aged Care and Disability Workers Vaccination) (COVID-19) Direction 2021, from 30 November 2021 both in-home and community aged care and disability support workers were required to have received at least one dose of a TGA-approved COVID-19 vaccination and have evidence of a booking to receive their second dose of the COVID-19 vaccine within an appropriate time interval.    Previous directions (first implemented on 24 November 2021 according to the Emergency Management (Residential Aged Care Facilities No 43) (COVID-19) Direction 2021) regarding the restriction of entry into residential aged care facilities, as well as general directions regarding the residential aged care workforce specified in H6 between 25-29 November 2021 continued to be in place.  Under these directions, unauthorised visitors, as well as those who had COVID-19 symptoms, had come into contact with a COVID-19 case or visited a high-risk area in the past 14 days, were waiting on a COVID-19 test result, were not wearing a mask, or were unvaccinated against COVID-19 and influenza were generally prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities. Residents of aged care facilities with a vaccination rate of under 70% could only receive a maximum of two care and support visitors per day. Workers operated under single-site restrictions (where possible), were required to wear PPE, and had to complete mandatory COVID-19 training. Aged care facilities also had to submit workforce management and infection control plans.    Thus, the directions introduced on 30 November regarding the vaccination of both in-home and community aged care workers were a tightening of existing restrictions, although all other restrictions were a continuation of existing directions. column33: There were no mentions of mandated requirements for public event cancellations, but COVID-safe measures for public activities and events were implemented. column69: According to the SA EntryCheck website as of 03 December 2021, and the Emergency Management (Arrivals Associated No 4) (COVID-19) Direction 2021 which was valid at the time:    Unvaccinated individuals older than 12 years and 2 months were prohibited from entering SA unless they had successfully applied for an exemption. All individuals travelling to SA were required to complete an EntryCheck SA application.    There were no further restrictions on arrivals from 'very low risk' areas with no evidence of COVID-19 community transmissions (e.g. Queensland, Tasmania, and Western Australia).       Arrivals from 'low risk' areas with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a full dose vaccination rate of 90% or higher (e.g. ACT and Victoria) were required to obtain a negative COVID-19 test result within 72 hours before arriving in SA, as well as undergo a daily symptom check for 14 days after arrival.    Arrivals from 'moderate risk' areas, or areas with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a full dose vaccination rate of 80% or more (e.g. NSW) were required to obtain a negative COVID-19 test result within 72 hours before arriving in SA, then quarantine until they took another mandatory COVID-19 test within 24 hours after arrival. They also needed to undergo a daily symptom check for 14 days after arrival.    Arrivals from 'high risk areas', or areas with evidence of COVID-19 community transmission and a full dose vaccination rate less than 80% were required to do the following:  	- obtain a negative COVID-19 test result within 72 hours before arriving in SA  	- Quarantine for 7 days after arrival  	- Take COVID-19 tests 24 hours, 6 days, and 13 days after arrival  	- Undergo daily symptom checks and avoid high risk settings and COVID Management Plan events during the 14 days after arrival    Individuals who had close contact with a COVID-19 case within 7 days before arriving in SA were prohibited from entering the state. Those who had close contact with a COVID-19 case within 14 days before arriving were required to get tested on the 13th day after contact.    Cross Border Community members from the NSW Cross Border Corridor or the Victorian Cross Border Corridor who had left their respective corridors for more than 72 hours and travelled to an LGA outside their Corridor were subject to additional testing and quarantine requirements depending on the risk level of the location they had travelled to. Cross Border Community members aged between 12 years and 2 months and 18 years could enter SA unvaccinated as long as they could provide evidence of a at least one COVID-19 vaccination with a second appointment booked by 8 December 2021.  Residents of Nhill were required to obtain a negative COVID-19 test within 72 hours of arriving in SA, or have evidence of a negative COVID-19 test taken within the past seven days if they had visited SA prior to arriving.    These restrictions were a continuation of the directions which came into effect on 2 December 2021. column90: The SA Government website did not specifically mention whether contact tracing was being conducted for all positive cases of COVID-19. column106: According to the South Australian government website, as of December 29, 2021  - Comirnaty (Pfizer) vaccine at a reduced dose is available for all people 5 to 11.  - Comirnaty (Pfizer) vaccine is available for all people 12+ years  - Spikevax (Moderna) vaccine is available for all people 12+ years at participating pharmacies.  - Vaxzevria (AstraZeneca) vaccine is available for people 18+ years at participating GPs and pharmacies.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220103115050/https://www.sahealth.sa.gov.au/wps/wcm/connect/public+content/sa+health+internet/conditions/infectious+diseases/covid-19/vaccine/getting+vaccinated/vaccination+hubs
column115: According to the South Australian government website, as of December 29, 2021, a person must not enter a Residential Aged Care Facility unless they have received at least one dose of a TGA approved or recognised COVID-19 vaccination; and received or have evidence of a booking to receive a second dose of a TGA approved COVID-19 vaccine. column24: There was no business closure policy during this time period. column33: There were public events restrictions in place during this time period, according to the framework for COVID safe events implemented in Dec 2020. column42: There was no new gathering restriction policy during this time period.   According to the Tas government COVID-19 webpage, gathering restrictions had last been updated from December 11 2020. Gathering limits are determined by the density of the area, up to a maximum of 250 people for an undivided space in an indoor premise; and 1,000 people in the outdoor space of premises. column51: There are no public transport closures during this period. Passengers are encouraged to keep physical distancing in mind and choose a seat away from others where possible. column60: There was no stay at home policy for Tasmania during this time period.   According to announcements on the Tasmanian Govt website, the last stay at home measures in place for Tas concluded in June 2020. This policy applied to the whole of Tas.  This policy had been in place prior to this time period, which was a maintenance of stay at home policy.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210331112824/http://www.premier.tas.gov.au/releases/stage_two_restrictions_begin_to_ease
column69: According to the Tasmanian Govt's official COVID-19 webpage, only travellers who have spent time in a high-risk domestic area or premise in the 14 days before arriving in Tasmania are not permitted to enter Tasmania unless approved as an Essential Traveller. Those not in high-risk areas were permitted to enter Tas provided they fill out a declaration through a Tas-e pass. There was no variation within Tas.  During this period there were a number of restrictions on inter-state travel. People who had visited high-risk premises in Victoria were essentially banned from entering the state while those who had visited Greater Sydney region, the Northern Beaches LGA and Wollongong LGA in NSW and Greater Brisbane in QLD were considered medium-risk and required to quarantine for 14 days (home quarantine was allowed).  This policy was the same compared with prior one.  It was not clear when the high risk areas would be deemed as non high risk areas.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210117034105/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania
column74: As published on the Department of Home Affairs website, no foreign arrivals are permitted into the country unless they are in an exempt category or have been granted an individual exemption which includes compassionate and national interest grounds. All international arrivals must quarantine for 14 days at a designated facility. There is the possibility to travel to Australia quarantine free without an exemption if you have been in New Zealand for 14 days or more and not been in a designated COVID-19 outbreak location, and you are travelling to Australia on a quarantine-free flight from 14/12/2020.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210101130014/https://covid19.homeaffairs.gov.au/travel-restrictions   https://web.archive.org/web/20201231084847/https://covid19.homeaffairs.gov.au/new-zealand-safe-travel-zone
column77: Individuals are able to receive a $150 coronavirus supplement per fortnight from 01/01/2021 which represents $100 less than the policy previous ending on 31/12/2020. column79: There was a range of debt/contract relief schemes offered by the Tasmanian govt. during this period.  The Tasmanian Government is providing rent relief for residential households who rent homes in the private market and who are experiencing housing stress because of the impact of the coronavirus (COVID-19). The COVID-19 Rent Relief Fund was established in May 2020 to help tenants and property owners suffering extreme hardship, with support of up to $2,000 or four weeks rent available. This policy was across Tas.  Many of the aforementioned policies had been in place for much of the pandmic. The Tasmanian Government extended the COVID-19 emergency period for residential tenancies to 31 January 2021, which will bring change to some policies mentioned above.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210308132647/https://www.cbos.tas.gov.au/topics/housing/residential-tenancies-covid-19-emergency-provisions
column86: On 4 February 2020, on the Premier and Cabinet's website, public health information is consistent with the Australian Government and refers to the state Department of Health and the Commonwealth Department of Health's websites regarding regular updates. Also, "Tasmania's Director of Public Health, Dr Mark Veitch, is providing regular updates to local GPs, hospitals and other sectors to ensure people who work in these settings are aware of the protocols in place to identify and manage a suspected case of coronavirus". column88: According to the Tasmanian Govt COVID-19 webpage in Dec 2020, testing was available to anyone symptomatic. column90: According to Tas Govt sources, Tasmania has maintained a comprehensive contact tracing regime for much of the pandemic. In Dec 2020, the government launched their check-in app for all customer facing business to utilise. Contact tracing records have been mandatory for premises where a lot of people will be spending an extended period of time (e.g. restaurants or cinemas) since 13 November 2020 whether through Chick in TAS or pen and paper. It is difficult to know how this would perform in practice if there were an outbreak. However, given Tasmania’s ability to control the virus so far, there is no reason to believe that with sensible policy responses to control the outbreak, that the contact tracing system wouldn’t be suitable. Contact tracing applied to all regions of Tasmania.   Much of the contact tracng policy came in during 2020, and it was not clear whether any changes had been made since or in the near future. column90: According to Tas Govt sources, Tasmania has maintained a comprehensive contact tracing regime for much of the pandemic. column79: On 16 March, tenant and landlord support are still in place. For example:  1) Private Rental Incentives Program: it helps eligible low income Tasmanians access affordable private rental properties. The program offers landlords an incentive to lease their homes for a two-year period at a rent that is set at an affordable level for clients off the Housing Register.    2) COVID-19 Rent Relief Fund: established to assist tenants suffering from extreme hardship, with support of up to $2,000 or four weeks rent available. More information on the Fund is available from the Communities Tasmania website.    3) Residential rent relief for social housing: The Tasmanian Government will not increase the rent for social housing tenants over the next six months, and will not count Federal Government COVID-19 emergency payments as income for the purposes of calculating rent contributions. If a household experiences a decrease in their household income, their rent will be decreased based on the Centrelink rates before the COVID-19 payments were established.    Any tenant whose income has been reduced as a result of the COVID-19 should contact their tenancy manager and their rents will be adjusted. column103: According to the "Requirement to wear masks at airports and on aircraft" document dated 28 January, indicates:  "All people aged 12 and older who are  at a Tasmanian airport, or on an aircraft must wear a facemask at all times.You must wear a mask when:  - inside or outside an airport terminal. This includes saying goodbye and greeting passengers (unless you stay in your car)  - on board your flight (including during boarding and disembarking, while flying, and when you are on the tarmac)  - waiting for your transport or walking to or from your transport (including in the car park)."    Also, according to the "Information for theatres and entertainment venues" document dated 16 March 2021, facemasks are required when:  - If being filled to 75 per cent of fixed seating capacity will cause the density to be more than one person per two square metres, there are two options: 1) Either everyone indoors at the event must wear a fitted face covering (unless they are exempt) – see below – or  2) the number of seated patrons must be lowered until the density limit is not exceeded.    Because using face coverings is optional when the seated capacity allows social distancing (one person per two square metres) this would be coded as a 2 (a 3 indicates wearing masks even when social distancing is possible). column15: According to the Tasmanian Department of Education website between 14 March and 11 April 2021, schoolchildren were not required to maintain social distancing, and were instead encouraged to adopt good hygiene practices. However, all adults working in schools were required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m, and school events were required to follow venue density requirements (one person per two square metres with a capacity limit of 250 individuals). School events which involved dancing were required to have separate areas for drinking and dancing.     Schools received extra cleaning of high-touch areas and toilets, as well as access to supplies such as soap, hand sanitiser, and disinfectant wipes.    Interstate and international excursions were cancelled, as were large sports and arts events with long lead time organisational arrangements.    The measures in place between 29 March and 11 April 2021 were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210314165549/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/  https://web.archive.org/web/20210411030917/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/
column24: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 30 March 2021, businesses and workplaces were permitted to operate as long as they adhered to minimum COVID-19 safety standards and recorded these in a COVID Safety Plan. Under these minimum standards, businesses were required to collect contact information from staff and patrons in order to assist with contact tracing efforts, ensure that physical distancing requirements were being met, ensure that workers who were required to quarantine or self-isolate did not enter the workplace, maintain a cleaning schedule, and manage the entry of individuals who were suspected of having COVID-19 or had COVID-19 symptoms.    A density rule of one person per two square metres applied to many venues, and there were capacity restrictions on events with more than 250 people attending. Masks were also required to be worn in airports, and at large indoor events with more than one person per two square metres.    The directions in place were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210330035253/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/business-restrictions  http://web.archive.org/web/20210330035315/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/covid-19-safe-workplaces-framework  http://web.archive.org/web/20210330133452/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework  http://web.archive.org/web/20210330035317/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/gatherings-density-and-physical-distancing  https://web.archive.org/web/20210330035250/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/facemasks

column15: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 15 April 2021, and the Tasmanian Department of Education website as of 11 April 2021, schoolchildren were not required to maintain social distancing, and were instead encouraged to adopt good hygiene practices. However, all adults working in schools were required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m, and school events were required to follow venue density requirements (one person per two square metres with a capacity limit of 250 individuals). School events which involved dancing were required to have separate areas for drinking and dancing.     Schools received extra cleaning of high-touch areas and toilets, as well as access to supplies such as soap, hand sanitiser, and disinfectant wipes.    Interstate and international excursions were cancelled, as were large sports and arts events with long lead time organisational arrangements.    The measures in place between 12 and 23 April 2021 were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210411030917/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/  https://web.archive.org/web/20210415112937/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/schools-and-childcare
column24: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 19 April 2021, businesses and workplaces were permitted to operate as long as they adhered to minimum COVID-19 safety standards and recorded these in a COVID Safety Plan. Under these minimum standards, businesses were required to collect contact information from staff and patrons in order to assist with contact tracing efforts, ensure that physical distancing requirements were being met, ensure that workers who were required to quarantine or self-isolate did not enter the workplace, maintain a cleaning schedule, and manage the entry of individuals who were suspected of having COVID-19 or had COVID-19 symptoms.    A density rule of one person per two square metres applied to many venues, and there were capacity restrictions on events with more than 250 people attending. Masks were also required to be worn in airports, and at large indoor events with more than one person per two square metres.    The directions in place were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  http://web.archive.org/web/20210419124353/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/business-restrictions  http://web.archive.org/web/20210419115740/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/covid-19-safe-workplaces-framework  http://web.archive.org/web/20210420142317/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework  http://web.archive.org/web/20210419111737/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/gatherings-density-and-physical-distancing  https://web.archive.org/web/20210424083239/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/face-masks
column33: The DIRECTION UNDER SECTION 16 (Mass gatherings - No. 3) continued to be in place. Under these directions, public gatherings and events could be held with some COVID-safe measures in place:    Seated religious and entertainment events were required to either limit attendees to 250 individuals or have a 75% capacity limit - whichever was stricter. Other venues were required to maintain a 75% maximum capacity limit for events attended by over 250 people. COVID safety plan requirements and mask requirements at large events with more than one person per two square metres were also implemented. column115: Between 23 April 2021 and 30 April 2021, the "Direction under Section 16 - Residential Aged Care Facilities - No. 11" is in place (Since 24 February 2021).    "Visits to residential aged care facilities are permitted for people providing care and support, with the following restrictions:  - Visitors must not have any symptoms of COVID-19, including fever (a temperature higher than 37.5 degrees), symptoms of fever (chills, night sweats), cough, sore throat, shortness of breath or loss of taste or smell.  - Unless an exemption has been granted (see below) visitors must not be in quarantine. That means they must not have:          - been in an area or premises identified as medium or high-risk for COVID-19 in the previous 14 days          - had contact with anyone known to have COVID-19, or reasonably suspected of having COVID-19, within the previous 14 days (except as part of their employment while wearing effective personal protective equipment)"    Archived web: https://web.archive.org/web/20210424083446/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/aged-care-facility-visits  Archived web: https://web.archive.org/web/20210423080848/https://coronavirus.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0024/126294/Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-No.-11.pdf

column15: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 24 April 2021, and the Tasmanian Department of Education website as of 11 April 2021, schoolchildren were not required to maintain social distancing, and were instead encouraged to adopt good hygiene practices. However, all adults working in schools were required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m, and school events were required to follow venue density requirements (one person per two square metres with a capacity limit of 250 individuals). School events which involved dancing were required to have separate areas for drinking and dancing.     Schools received extra cleaning of high-touch areas and toilets, as well as access to supplies such as soap, hand sanitiser, and disinfectant wipes.    Interstate and international excursions were cancelled, as were large sports and arts events with long lead time organisational arrangements.    The measures in place between 26 and 30 April 2021 were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20210411030917/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/  https://web.archive.org/web/20210424083356/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/schools-and-childcare
column24: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 24 April 2021, businesses and workplaces were permitted to operate as long as they adhered to minimum COVID-19 safety standards and recorded these in a COVID Safety Plan. Under these minimum standards, businesses were required to collect contact information from staff and patrons in order to assist with contact tracing efforts, ensure that physical distancing requirements were being met, ensure that workers who were required to quarantine or self-isolate did not enter the workplace, maintain a cleaning schedule, and manage the entry of individuals who were suspected of having COVID-19 or had COVID-19 symptoms.    A density rule of one person per two square metres applied to many venues, and there were capacity restrictions on events with more than 250 people attending. Masks were also required to be worn in airports, and at large indoor events with more than one person per two square metres.    The directions in place were a continuation of existing directions. column33: The DIRECTION UNDER SECTION 16 (Mass gatherings - No. 3) continued to be in place. column51: According to the Tasmanian Government website and the Tasmanian Government transport services website as of March and April 2021, buses were subject to increased cleaning, with a focus on high-touch surfaces. column42: -	Gatherings are limited to 250 people per undivided space indoors, and 1000 people per undivided space outdoors, and a one person per 2 square metres rule also applies. Attendees should maintain a 1.5-metre distance from others if possible. These restrictions have applied since at least 9 July 2021; see https://web.archive.org/web/20210904031041/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/gatherings-density-and-physical-distancing.   -	Events that follow the Tasmanian Government's Framework for COVID-Safe Events and Activities (see https://web.archive.org/web/20210831035339/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework) may apply for increased attendance limits of up to 1000 (indoor, unseated), 2000 (indoor, seated), 5000 (outdoor, unseated) or 10,000 people (outdoor, seated). Gatherings at cinemas, theatres, convert venues, places of worship, funeral homes, stadiums, or arenas may host up to 100% seated capacity without specific government approval, provided that density limits are followed in non-seated areas, QR code check-ins are used, and a COVID-19 safety plan is followed.
column60: As of 24 August 2021, Tasmania is not in lockdown. The government is preparing for a potential lockdown if the Delta variant of COVID-19 is detected in the community. See http://web.archive.org/web/20210907175908/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/lockdown-plan.
column69: -	The Tasmanian government designates regions of Australia and New Zealand as low, medium or high risk.   -	Low-risk travellers (who have not been in medium or high-risk areas or premises in the past 14 days) should register their travel and contact details through the Tas e-Travel system, but are not required to quarantine.   -	Medium-risk travellers (who have not been to high-risk areas or premises) must complete a G2G pass and quarantine for 14 days in suitable premises.   -	High-risk travellers are not permitted to enter Tasmania unless they have received an exemption as essential travellers, and if permitted to enter, must quarantine in government-designated facilities (high-risk level 1) or in suitable premises (high-risk level 2).  -	As of August 24, the ACT, NSW, Victoria, and New Zealand are considered high risk. All other Australian states and territories are low-risk (except for specific premises).  -	Aside from changes in the risk levels of specific states and territories, this represents a continuation of restrictions in place since at least November 2020. See https://web.archive.org/web/20210831222422/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania.

column88: Anyone who has common COVID-19 symptoms (e.g. fever, runny nose, cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, loss of taste/smell) is encouraged to get tested for COVID-19. In addition, testing is also recommended for people at high risk of exposure (e.g. health care, aged care, or transport workers) showing less typical symptoms of COVID-19, and their household members who are showing symptoms.     In general only people with cold-like or flu-like symptoms, who are essential travellers, or who have been asked to get tested by Public Health (e.g. people possibly exposed during an outbreak) are entitled to free COVID-19 testing. Asymptomatic people who do not meet these criteria (e.g. who need to get tested for non-essential travel) may receive testing from a GP, but it is not provided for free by the government.  See https://web.archive.org/web/20210903075722/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/testing-for-covid19-faqs.
column90: -	Comprehensive contact tracing did not take place at this time, as there was no community transmission of COVID-19. column115: Under the Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions No.15, which was in force from 19–26 August 2021, there are restrictions on who may enter aged care facilities. People must not enter unless they are:   - residents  - employees or contractors at the facility  - providing goods or services to the facility or a resident  - providing care or support to a resident (including end-of-life support, or treatment for a medical condition)  - present for emergency management or law enforcement.  In addition, even if they fall within these categories of permitted visitors, people must not enter if they:  -  have been in a medium or high-risk COVID-19 area in the past 14 days  - have been in contact with a person suspected or confirmed to have COVID-19 in the past 14 days  - have symptoms of COVID-19  - or are required to isolate.  Visitors to aged-care facilities must generally wear masks while at the facility, unless they are under 12 years old, or have medical or other exemptions.   See pages 10-12 of http://web.archive.org/web/20220210011919/https://www.gazette.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/586980/22117_-_Gazette_1_September_2021.pdf.

Under the Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions No.16, in effect as of 11:59 pm on 26 August 2021, there are restrictions on who may enter aged care facilities. People must not enter unless they are:   - residents  - employees or contractors at the facility  - providing goods or services to the facility or a resident  - providing care or support to a resident (including end-of-life support, or treatment for a medical condition)  - present for emergency management or law enforcement.  In addition, even if they fall within these categories of permitted visitors, people must not enter if they:   - have been in a medium or high-risk COVID-19 area in the past 14 days;   - have been in contact with a person suspected or confirmed to have COVID-19 in the past 14 days;   - have symptoms of COVID-19;   - or are required to isolate.  These restrictions on entry are a continuation of previous rules. A previous requirement for most visitors to wear masks was revoked.  See pages 3–5 of https://web.archive.org/web/20220210034144/https://www.gazette.tas.gov.au/editions/2021/september_2021/22119_-_Gazette_8_September_2021.pdf.

column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418. - The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments  https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment

column77: -	People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. As of 7 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments.

column88: On October 1, 2021, the Tasmanian government has a dedicated website about "Testing for COVID-19" where people can find the different COVID-19 Testing Clinics around the state. According to the website, "testing for COVID-19 remains to be generally available to everyone able to get one.  The Tasmanian Government has a number of testing clinics, including a drive-through centre and a mobile testing van".    According to the FAQs website "testing is only available free if you have cold or flu symptoms, loss of taste/smell or have been asked by Public Health or required under Essential Traveller status to get tested. If you want to get tested but have no symptoms of COVID-19 and Public Health has not asked you to get tested, talk to your GP. There will be a charge for the test and your consultation with the GP". Also, the website states that "the main reason for targeting people with symptoms and people at high risk of exposure to the virus is that they are more likely to have COVID-19 than others. People with symptoms are also more likely to pass the virus on to other people than those who don’t."    According to the interpretation guide, testing announced as available for all symptomatic could indicate a "2", while announcing that anyone interested in getting a test could indicate a "3". And due to the emphasis on symptomatic people, this should be coded as a "2". column24: As of 15 October 2021, there is no requirements for business attendees or visitors to provide proof of vaccination when they enter businesses. Workplaces are operating but they must have a "COVID-19 Safety Plan that complies with minimum COVID-19 standards" in line with the "DIRECTION UNDER SECTION 16 (Workplace COVIDPlan - No. 2) dated 18 December 2020. The Minimum Standards require all workplaces to:   -	manage the risks of a person contracting or spreading COVID-19 in the workplace.   -	implement and maintain a cleaning schedule across the workplace.   -	have good hygiene procedures and practices (such as washing and/or sanitising of hands).   -	make sure physical distancing requirements are met by workers, contractors and others entering, leaving or moving around the workplace.     However, between 6 pm 15 October and 6 pm 18 October 2021, Southern Tasmania went into lockdown. Changes in the density of people allowed - one person per four square metres —  will apply in most businesses and premises that remain open (with some exemptions, eg airports, passenger transport). Cafes, restaurants and hotels would be open for takeaway only. Supermarkets remained open but clothing stores "can provide contactless collection only. column77: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. There is also a COVID-19 Disaster Payment, a lump sum payment for workers unable to earn an income due to state or territory public health orders (e.g. a lockdown). The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week. column77: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. There is also a COVID-19 Disaster Payment, a lump sum payment for workers unable to earn an income due to state or territory public health orders (e.g. a lockdown). The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week.
