Unless an exemption has been granted by the facility in relation to end-of-life care.  - The operators of aged care facilities are required to record the contact details for everyone who enters the facility regardless of length of visit.  - If visits are being carried out in communal areas, it is important that a physical distance of 1.5 metres be maintained between people whenever possible.    More details can be found from the web archive link below. This represents a continuation of policy response to Covid-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211108054723/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/aged-care-facility-visits

column79: There is limited debt or contract relief provided to Tasmanians.  This includes lowering home loans and allowing payment deferral.    Therefore, it should be reported as 1.    Archived link: https://web.archive.org/web/20211214035633/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/financial-services-and-support
column86: The Tasmanian Government has a comprehensive public health campaign that is currently operating. The Government uses both traditional sources of media, such as a hotline and posters, as well as social media, as seen from their Facebook page.    Therefore, it should be reported as 2G.    Archived link: https://archive.ph/7xjeg
column88: According to the Tasmanian Government, There are four different ways to get a COVID-19 test in Tasmania:  1. COVID-19 drive through Testing Clinics in Hobart, Launceston, Devonport and Burnie – this option is free.  2. GP-led respiratory clinics in a general practice setting in Hobart, Launceston and St Helens – this option is free.  3. Mobile testing clinics that move around Tasmania – this option is free.  4. Your local GP clinic if they offer COVID-19 testing – GPs may charge a consultation fee.    GP-led respiratory clinics are currently able to see people who are asymptomatic. Generally, these clinics are for people who have mild-to-moderate cold and flu symptoms. They provide assessment, testing, and initial treatment of symptoms. These clinics are free, including for people who are not covered by Medicare. You don’t need a doctor’s referral to go to these free clinics, but you do need to make an appointment. Don’t just turn up.    Therefore, it should be reported as 3.    Archived link: http://web.archive.org/web/20211108054651/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/testing-for-covid19-faqs
column90: According to the Tasmanian Government (published on 29 Nov 2021), Public Health will continue to respond to cases, monitor the health of cases, and trace people required to quarantine, to reduce the spread. Public Health will continue to identify people  who come into contact with positive cases, while infectious in the community by:  • interviewing positive cases about where they’ve been and who they may have come into contact with while infectious; and  • working with workplaces and exposure sites, and using the Check in Tas App data to identify people who may have been at risk of exposure.    Additionally, using Check in TAS is mandatory in Tasmania for contact tracing since 1 May 2021 (see below).    Therefore, it should be reported as 2.    Archived link: https://web.archive.org/web/20211130235539/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0024/196044/Keeping-our-community-safe_v3.0.pdf  https://archive.ph/XipMW  https://archive.ph/My4BE  https://archive.ph/M0htD
column103: According to the Tasmanian Government, facial masks are required in some public spaces. From 18 September 2021, masks are required to be worn at any event that has more than 1000 people in attendance, regardless of whether the event is seated or unseated, indoors or outdoors.    Where masks are required, there may be some exceptions to wearing one, including:  - Children aged under 12 years or those undertaking primary education  - While doing certain activities, so long as the mask is replaced once those activities are finished  - Anyone who has medical certification (or other documentation from a medical practitioner) of a physical or mental health, condition or disability that makes wearing a fitted mask unsuitable.    Therefore, it should be reported as 2G.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211209085451/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/face-masks  http://web.archive.org/web/20211214233847/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/face-masks/face-masks-at-events-and-gatherings
column106: According to the Department of Health (Commonwealth) (updated on 28 Oct 2021), COVID-19 vaccination is free for everyone in Australia, even if people don't have a Medicare card.    Therefore, it should be reported as 5G.    Archived link: https://archive.ph/9hQDZ

column15: As of 29 November 2021, All schools continue to operate full-time learning at school. There is no vaccination mandatory for students to attend school and all students should be at school unless: they have medical advice which states that they are unable to return to school due to an ongoing medical condition and the expected timeframe they are currently unwell. Any flu, cold, hay fever, and covid-19 symptoms are hard to tell so that students experiencing such symptoms (such as runny/blocked nose, sneezing, itchy eyes or cough), even mild symptoms, should get tested.     School students do not need to follow strict adult physical distancing guidelines. They should follow good hygiene practices like: staying home when you are sick, regularly washing your hands, avoid sharing drinks or food, cough or sneeze into your elbow, or a tissue which should be discarded immediately. No face mask and check-in requirements at schools. This represents a continuation of policy response to Covid-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211001061435/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/    https://web.archive.org/web/20211228050615/https://www.premier.tas.gov.au/covid-19_updates/press_conference_-_22_october_2021
column24: As of 29 November 2021, there is no requirements for business attendees or visitors to provide proof of vaccination when they enter businesses, however, workplaces are operating but they must have a "COVID-19 Safety Plan that complies with minimum COVID-19 standards" in line with the "DIRECTION UNDER SECTION 16 (Workplace COVIDPlan - No. 2) dated 18 December 2020.     The Minimum Standards require all workplaces to:   -	manage the risks of a person contracting or spreading COVID-19 in the workplace.   -	implement and maintain a cleaning schedule across the workplace.   -	have good hygiene procedures and practices (such as washing and/or sanitising of hands).   -	make sure physical distancing requirements are met by workers, contractors and others entering, leaving or moving around the workplace.     This represents a continuation of policy response to Covid-19.     https://web.archive.org/web/20211001061703/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/covid-19-safe-workplaces-framework    https://web.archive.org/web/20211009235706/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/91238/Workplace-COVID-Plan-No.-2-18-Dec-20.pdf
column33: As of 29 November 2021, there is no requirement for public events attendees to provide proof of vaccination to enter and attend events in Tasmania. However, all events require an Events COVID-19 Safety Plan. Face masks are required to be worn at any event that is expected to have more than 1,000 people in attendance, physical distancing, gathering sizes and density limits, and contact details for patrons. Tasmania is still using the "DIRECTION UNDER SECTION 16" (Mass gatherings - No. 4) commenced on 1 May 2021 and it is still in place.    This represents a continuation of the policy response to Covid-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004005620/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework    https://web.archive.org/web/20211009155831/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/267151/A_Framework_for_COVID-19_Safe_Events_and_Activities_in_Tasmania_-_version_2.pdf
column42: The Tasmanian Government declared a maximum gathering limits of 250 people in an indoor venue and 500 people in an outdoor venue. The maximum density rule of 2 square metres per person applies. If the number of people permitted according to the density limit is less than the gathering limit, the lower number applies. There was also a limit of 100 people allowed to gather on residential premises. This was a continuation of existing policy.    See https://web.archive.org/web/20211209091524/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/gatherings-density-and-physical-distancing
column51: As of 29 November 2021, there is no requirement for public transport users to provide proof of vaccination when they enter public transports in Tasmania. However, there are some restrictions in place that: passengers are encouraged to keep physical distancing in mind and choose a seat away from others where possible, avoid touching surfaces inside the bus whenever you can, adults seeking to board a bus which has a high number of passengers are asked to consider waiting for the next service where available, and comply with any requests from your bus driver.    This represents a continuation of policy response to Covid-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004010353/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/transport
column60: As of 29 November 2021, there is no requirement for residents who are not vaccinated to stay at home or are not permitted to leave home in Tasmania. Face masks and social distancing are not required at this time. There may be restrictions in place if the whole State or regional areas go into lockdown according to Tasmania lockdown plan.    This represents a continuation of policy response to Covid-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210930063108/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/lockdown-plan
column69: As of 29 November 2021, there is no requirement for inbound travellers to provide proof of vaccination in Tasmania. However, restrictions on internal movement are in place. "Travellers to Tasmania, including returning residents, need to provide their contact and travel details before entering the State, to help manage the risk of COVID-19 at Tasmania’s borders".     This represents a continuation of policy response to Covid-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211001205029/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania
column74: As of 29 November 2021, there is a vaccination requirement in place for overseas and Tasmanian residents’ travellers who intend to come to Tasmania.    Travelling directly to Tasmania from overseas:   - Travellers who have been overseas (other than low-risk areas in New Zealand, or approved Australian Antarctic Division travellers) or on a cruise ship in the 14 days prior to arriving in Tasmania, must quarantine for 14 days on arrival in Tasmania.  - Overseas arrivals must be fully vaccinated and also have two COVID-19 tests while in quarantine – the first will occur within 48 hours of arrival, and the second will be on or soon after day 12 of quarantine.    http://web.archive.org/web/20211129195439/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania

column15: According to the Tasmanian Government Department of Education website as of 9 December 2021, students were expected to attend classes in person, and there was no requirement for students to practice social distancing. However, some COVID-safe measures were implemented in schools:    Interstate and international excursions were cancelled , and large arts and sports events with long lead time organisational arrangements were delayed or cancelled.  School celebrations and social events were required to follow a density requirement of one person per two square metres up to a maximum of 250 people. Events which involved dancing were required to have separate areas for dancing and consuming food.   All adults visiting and working in schools were to maintain a physical distance of 1.5 metres.  Schools received extra cleaning in high-touch areas and toilets, and received extra cleaning supplies.    The directions in place were a continuation of existing directions.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211209083612/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/
column69: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated 1 December 2021), travellers who had spent time in high-risk Australian jurisdictions (such as NSW, the ACT, and Victoria) in the past 14 days were prohibited from entering Tasmania unless they had obtained approval to enter the state for essential reasons. Approved travellers from high-risk jurisdictions were required to quarantine at a suitable premises or at a government-managed facility. Travellers from high-risk areas wishing to enter Tasmania were required to apply for a G2G pass.    Travellers who had only spent time in low-risk areas (such as Queensland and WA) in the past 14 days were not required to quarantine upon arrival, although they were directed to register their trip and contact details through the Tas-e-travel system.     This was a continuation of existing directions    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211209084037/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania  https://web.archive.org/web/20211130085202/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania
column74: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 13 December 2021, overseas travellers were prohibited from entering Tasmania unless they had obtained pre-approval from the Deputy State Controller. Typically, only applications from vaccinated Tasmanians and specialist workers were approved.    Overseas travellers who were able to enter Tasmania were required to quarantine for 14 days and take COVID-19 tests 2 days and 12 days after arrival.  This was a continuation of existing restrictions.     https://web.archive.org/web/20211213214634/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania
column115: Some narrow restrictions on visitors exist on aged care services. column24: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated 19 November 2021), all businesses may remain open, but Covid-safe measures apply. For example, most businesses must comply with limits on density and large gatherings, and implement QR code check-ins to assist contact tracing. This is a continuation of previous policies.   See https://web.archive.org/web/20211209091417/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/business-restrictions.     Furthermore, as of 6 December 2021, all patrons at pubs, bars, nightclubs and licensed events where alcohol is served and people can freely mix and move (i.e. are not seated) must be fully vaccinated, and density limits continue to apply to these venues. For unvaccinated people, this is a tightening of previous policy. See https://web.archive.org/web/20220128042741/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/vaccination-requirements/pubs-bars-nightclubs-and-licensed-events.
column33: As of 6 December 2021, all patrons at pubs, bars, nightclubs and licensed events where alcohol is served and people can freely mix and move (i.e. are not seated) must be fully vaccinated, and density limits continue to apply to these venues. This was a tightening of previous restrictions for the unvaccinated.    Other COVID-safe event restrictions remained the same:  Organisers of "tier 1" events (250–2000 people indoors, or 500–2000 people outdoors) must complete a COVID-19 checklist and register the event with the Director of Public Health. Organisers of larger events (i.e. higher than tier 1) must implement a COVID-19 safety plan that is approved by the Director of Public Health. In addition, all large events must comply with a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres and use QR code check-ins. Masks were required at large events with over 1000 attendees.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220128042741/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/business-and-employees/vaccination-requirements/pubs-bars-nightclubs-and-licensed-events.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211110160038/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework  https://web.archive.org/web/20220111225748/https://www.business.tas.gov.au/coronavirus_information/event_framework  http://web.archive.org/web/20220205102920/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/133074/Direction-under-Section-16-Mass-gatherings-No.-6.pdf.

column15: As of 9 December 2021, schools are open full-time. However basic hygiene measures such as hand washing, staying home when sick, and avoiding the sharing of food or drinks are encouraged. Interstate and international excursions have been cancelled. Certain large social events may go ahead, subject to density limits and hygiene measures. This is a continuation of conditions since at least August 2020 (barring local lockdowns). See https://web.archive.org/web/20211209083612/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/.
column42: -	Gatherings at residential premises must not exceed 100 people, while gatherings at stadiums, arenas, cinemas and theatres, concert venues, and places of worship must not exceed 250 people. Outdoor gatherings are limited to 250 people. In addition, a density limit of one person per 2 square metres applies. This is a continuation of rules since 6 December 2021. More details at http://web.archive.org/web/20211227134542/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0030/196086/Management-of-premises-No-16.pdf.   -	Gatherings that exceed the 250/500 person limit must follow the COVID-19 Events Framework (https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0026/191762/Events-Framework-October-2021.pdf). Under this framework, "tier 1" events (up to 2,000 people) must complete a COVID-19 checklist and use QR code check-ins. Larger gatherings must be approved by the Director of Public Health, implement a COVID-19 safety plan, and use QR code check-ins.
column51: Public transport continues to operate as normal in Tasmania. However, COVID-safe measures are encouraged, including but not limited to: social distancing where possible, travelling outside peak hours, avoiding public transport when unwell, good hand hygiene, cashless payment of fares, and QR code check-ins. See https://web.archive.org/web/20211209092004/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/transport.
column60: As of 14 December 2021, household gatherings of up to 100 people are permitted, implying that there are no stay-at-home orders in place. This is a continuation of policy since at least 19 November 2021, and remained current through at least January 2022. See https://web.archive.org/web/20220111215901/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/gatherings-density-and-physical-distancing.
column69: Areas within Australia are classified as low, medium, or high risk. Travellers who have only spent time in low-risk areas in the previous 14 days may enter without quarantine. Travellers from medium-risk areas must quarantine in "suitable premises" for 14 days. Trevellers from high-risk areas must not enter Tasmania unless granted an exemption, and must quarantine in government-managed facilities (high-risk level 1) or suitable premises (high-risk level 2). All travellers must register their travel, either through Tas e-Travel (low-risk) or through the G2G pass system (medium or high risk). See https://web.archive.org/web/20211213214634/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania.
column77: The Tasmanian Government's Pandemic Isolation Assistance Grant is a $250 payment for Tasmanians who miss work because they are isolating while awaiting a test result. Close contacts and confirmed COVID-19 cases who lose income as a result of being directed to quarantine, and who are not receiving the Australian Government's Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment, may receive a grant of $750 per week spent in quarantine from the Tasmanian Government. Returning Tasmanian residents who must quarantine, cannot earn income as a result, and are not receiving Australian Government income support are also eligible for grants from the Tasmanian Government ($750 per week spent in quarantine). The larger $750 grants are more than half Tasmania's median household income of $1,100 (see 2016 census stats: http://web.archive.org/web/20220205110559/https://quickstats.censusdata.abs.gov.au/census_services/getproduct/census/2016/quickstat/6?opendocument). For more information on the grants, see  https://web.archive.org/web/20211218215349/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/individual-grants
column79: Narrow debt/contract relief measures, including a moratorium on evictions and rent increases, and the ability to reduce rent by mutual agreement, are in place as of December 2021. See https://web.archive.org/web/20211214035633/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/families-community/financial-services-and-support.
column86: The Tasmanian government runs a coordinated public information campaign through its website (http://web.archive.org/web/20211209085739/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/). The site provides regular updates on COVID-19 in Tasmania, in addition to resources regarding current restrictions and guidelines, rules for travel to Tasmania, economic support for affected people and businesses, testing and vaccination, and other information related to COVID-19 in Tasmania.
column88: -	The Tasmanian Government website, which was last updated on 8 November 2021 and remained current as of 5 December 2021 (see https://web.archive.org/web/20211205111017/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/keeping-yourself-safe/testing-for-covid19-faqs) stated that anyone who has common COVID-19 symptoms (e.g. fever, runny nose, cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, loss of taste/smell) is encouraged to get tested for COVID-19. In addition, testing is also recommended for people at high risk of exposure (e.g. health care, aged care, or transport workers) showing less typical symptoms of COVID-19, and their household members who are showing symptoms.   -	In general only people with cold-like or flu-like symptoms, who are essential travellers, or who have been asked to get tested by Public Health (e.g. people possibly exposed during an outbreak) are entitled to free COVID-19 testing. Asymptomatic people who do not meet these criteria (e.g. who need to get tested for non-essential travel) may receive testing, but it is not provided for free by the government.  -	Premier Peter Gutwein advised in a later press conference on 30 December 2021 that PCR tests should be reserved for those with symptoms or who returned a positive RAT, which would represent a continuation of policy through that date, including the period from 10-17 December 2021. (https://web.archive.org/web/20211231073605/https://www.premier.tas.gov.au/site_resources_2015/additional_releases/national_cabinet_update)
column103: As of 9 December 2021, Tasmanians must wear masks in certain public settings. These include airports and commercial aircraft, Spirit of Tasmania ferries, when approved to leave quarantine, after arriving in Tasmania from interstate COVID-19 hotspots, at large events and gatherings over 1000 people, and in health care settings. column106: All Tasmanian residents aged 12 years and over are eligible for a free COVID-19 vaccination. column115: -	Under the Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions No.16, in effect as of 11:59 pm on 26 August 2021, there are restrictions on who may enter aged care facilities.  -	People must not enter unless they are: residents, employees or contractors at the facility; providing goods or services to the facility or a resident; providing care or support to a resident (including end-of-life support, or treatment for a medical condition); present for emergency management or law enforcement.  -	In addition, even if they fall within these categories of permitted visitors, people must not enter if they: have been in a medium or high-risk COVID-19 area in the past 14 days; have been in contact with a person suspected or confirmed to have COVID-19 in the past 14 days; have symptoms of COVID-19; or are required to isolate.  -	These restrictions on entry are a continuation of previous rules. See https://web.archive.org/web/20211213214634/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania.
column115: Under the Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions No.17, in effect as of 15 December 2021, there are restrictions on who may enter aged care facilities.  -	People must not enter unless they are: residents, employees or contractors at the facility; providing goods or services to the facility or a resident; providing care or support to a resident; present for emergency management or law enforcement.  -	In addition, even if they fall within these categories of permitted visitors, people must not enter if they: have been in a medium or high-risk COVID-19 area in the past 14 days; have been in contact with a person suspected or confirmed to have COVID-19 in the past 14 days; have symptoms of COVID-19; or are required to isolate.  -	Two new requirements were introduced beginning on 15 December 2021. column15: A continuation of the existing policy, schools remained open with all children expected to attend school in-person unless they were unwell, were told to remain at home on medical advice, or were directed to stay home by Public Health. The following recommendations are in place to help slow the spread of COVID-19. This means: staying at home when you’re sick and getting tested regular handwashing and sanitising avoid sharing drinks or food   In addition to this, there was frequent cleaning in schools, particularly  high-touch surfaces. Schools were given access to more soap, hand sanitiser, paper towels and disinfectant wipes.   All adults were required to maintain a 1.5m physical distance from one another.  School-based interstate and international travel were also cancelled.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211227181431/https://www.education.tas.gov.au/parents-carers/novel-coronavirus-covid-19/learning-at-school-parents-and-carers-guide/

column33: For events deemed to be “small gatherings” (up to 250 people indoors or 500 people outdoors), there are no requirements in addition to general state-wide gathering requirements. column69: Individuals could register to travel to Tasmania without a test requirement or needing to quarantine if they:  • were fully vaccinated  • had not been in any high or extreme-risk areas in the 14 days before arriving in Tasmania.   Unvaccinated individuals were required to successfully apply for an approval in order to enter Tasmania. This process involved presenting evidence of a negative COVID-19 PCR test taken in the 72 hours prior to departure. Unvaccinated travellers who were allowed to enter Tasmania were required to arrive at approved entry points and take COVID-19 tests on day 1 and day 5 after arrival. They were also required to quarantine at suitable premises for a minimum of 5 days, or a maximum of 14 days.  Fully vaccinated individuals who had been in a high-risk area 14 days before intending to arrive in Tasmania were required to return a negative result from a COVID 19 PCR test taken in the 72 hours prior.  This was a continuation of existing directions.   https://web.archive.org/web/20211222120905/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania/extreme-high-and-low-risk-areas https://web.archive.org/web/20211222120954/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania/fully-vaccinated-travellers https://web.archive.org/web/20211222121002/https://www.coronavirus.tas.gov.au/travellers-and-visitors/coming-to-tasmania/unvaccinated-travellers
column77: The Tasmanian Government offered several different income support payments for eligible Tasmanians affected by COVID-19:   - Eligible Tasmanians who were at risk of losing income due to a COVID-19 vaccine appointment, side effects from receiving a COVID-19 vaccine, or due to caring for a dependant who received a COVID-19 vaccine, could receive a $250 lump sum payment.    - A Pandemic Leave Isolation Grant offered by the Tasmanian Government was also available to Tasmanians under the following circumstances: 	• unable to receive the Federal Government's Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment, they could receive a lump sum of $750 for every seven days they had to isolate 	• When unvaccinated Tasmanian residents returning from interstate or overseas were required to self-isolate, they could receive a lump sum of $750 for every seven days they were required to quarantine 	• When support workers or self-employed individuals were required to isolate due to COVID-19 risk, they could call the Public Health Hotline to receive the grant. column24: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as of 9 December 2021 and as last updated on 4 January 2022), all businesses were permitted to operate, but were required to adopt measures to meet minimum COVID-19 safety standards as stated in the Direction under Section 16 - COVID-19 Workplace Plans - No.2, and record these in a safety plan. As part of these minimum safety standards, businesses were required to practice 1.5m social distancing or impose a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres (although exempted workplaces were only required to ensure that the number of individuals in the workplace did not exceed the number specified on their occupancy permits), maintain cleaning and hygiene practices workplace to minimise the spread of COVID-19, train and inform staff and patrons of COVID-safe requirements they must follow in order to minimise transmission, prevent individuals who had COVID-19 symptoms or were known to be under isolation requirements from entering the premises, and collect contact information from individuals entering or leaving the workplace in order to assist with contact tracing efforts.     Masks were also required in indoor spaces. Individuals entering pubs, nightclubs, bars, and some licensed events were required to be fully vaccinated. Other industry-specific COVID-safe guidelines, such as regular COVID-19 testing for those working in quarantine facilities, and the adoption of transmission-based precautions  in healthcare settings were also in place.     The restrictions in place between 29 December 2021 and 5 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 directions. column33: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as of 14 December 2021 and as last updated on 4 January 2022), and the Direction under Section 16 - Mass gatherings - No.6, public events were allowed to go ahead as long as they adhered to density and COVID-safe guidelines. Event organisers were to ensure that, where possible, attendees could maintain a physical distance of 1.5m. They were also required to maintain a maximum density of 1 person per 2 square metres. Masks were generally required indoors and for events with over 1000 people attending.     A multi-tiered system for regulating public events based on the number of expected attendees and the activity type was also in place: Tier 1 events, which consisted of indoor events with 251-2000 people, and outdoor events with 501-2000 people who were free to move around or be seated, were required to have an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and utilise Check In Tas QR codes. Some indoor events attended by over 250 people also had to be registered with Business Tasmania.   Tier 2 events, which consisted of all events with 2,001-5,000 people who were free to move around and be seated, as well as tier 3 events, which consisted of all higher-risk activities and seated events with 5,001-10,000 people, were required to complete an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan and Event registration. These events had to be approved by the Director of Public Health in order to occur, and also needed to utilise Check In Tas QR codes.     Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, and outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate, Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health.     The directions in place between 29 December 2021 and 5 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. They were also required to maintain a maximum density of 1 person per 2 square metres. Masks were generally required indoors and for events with over 1000 people attending.     The maximum number of individuals allowed to attend events without applying for approval was 250 individuals for undivided indoor spaces and 500 for outdoor events.     A multi-tiered system for regulating public events based on the number of expected attendees and the activity type was also in place:     Tier 1 events, which consisted of indoor events with 251-2000 people, and outdoor events with 501-2000 people who were free to move around or be seated, were required to have an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and utilise Check In Tas QR codes. Some indoor events attended by over 250 people also had to be registered with Business Tasmania.     Tier 2 events, which consisted of all events with 2,001-5,000 people who were free to move around and be seated, as well as tier 3 events, which consisted of all higher-risk activities and seated events with 5,001-10,000 people, were required to complete an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan and Event registration. These events had to be approved by the Director of Public Health in order to occur, and also needed to utilise Check In Tas QR codes.     The directions in place between 29 December 2021 and 5 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. column69: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as of 23 December 2021), unvaccinated individuals (including Tasmanian residents, and excluding those with a medical exemption from taking a COVID-19 vaccine, as well as children under 12 years and two months) required approval in order to enter the state, and had to obtain a negative PCR result within the 72 hours before departure. They were only allowed to enter the state at approved ports, take COVID-19 tests on day 1 and day 5 after arrival, and quarantine for either 5 or 14 days depending on the results of these tests.     Fully vaccinated travellers who had been to high risk locations (the ACT, and parts of NSW and Victoria) in the past 14 days were required to obtain a negative PCR test in the 72 hours prior to departure, or quarantine until they were able to obtain evidence of this negative PCR test. Those who had been outside of Tasmania for 7 days or fewer and had entered a high-risk location during this time were able to get a PCR test in the 72 hours prior to arrival without needing to quarantine before receiving the test result.     All testing requirements applied to travellers 5 years old and over.     Fully vaccinated travellers who had not been to any high-risk locations in the past 14 days were exempt from all testing and quarantine requirements. Those from low-risk jurisdictions were able to transit at some approved locations in high-risk jurisdictions before entering Tasmania, without being subject to testing and quarantine requirements.     All travellers were required to register on the Tas-e-travel and scan QR codes on arrival.     The directions in place between 29 December 2021 and 31 December 2021 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. column88: There was a lack of archived Tasmanian Government websites with comprehensive information regarding COVID-19 testing relevant to this time period (29 December 2021 to 5 January 2022).    In a media release published by the Premier of Tasmania on 30 December 2021, PCR tests would be prioritised for Tasmanians experiencing COVID-19 symptoms or those who had received a positive rapid antigen test result*. It is unclear whether this was also the case prior to 30 December 2021, but a Tasmanian Government website (as of 9 December 2021) stated that all Tasmanians experiencing COVID-19 symptoms should get a COVID-19 test.    Nonetheless, an ABC News report published on 30 December 2021 described surges in demand for PCR testing as COVID-19 cases in Tasmania continued to rise, leading to long queues at testing clinics, delays, and early testing clinic closures. *Although the report quoted the Tasmanian Premier stating that only symptomatic individuals should be receiving PCR tests from 1 January 2022 onwards, it also quoted the Tasmanian Premier mentioning that the State would "pivot to rapid antigen testing for those that are either symptomatic or haven't had a positive rapid antigen test already". As such, it was unclear whether every single symptomatic individual received a PCR test.    News reports and media releases published during this period of time indicate that the Tasmanian Government was intending to relax existing COVID-19 directions by narrowing eligibility criteria for PCR testing, and promoting the use of RATs among asymptomatic individuals who were required to take a COVID-19 test. column90: According to a COVID-19 update published by the Tasmanian Government on 26 December 2021, Tasmanian Public Health Services would be relying on individuals with COVID-19 to inform their close contacts and household contacts that they had been infected. Individuals with COVID-19 were also asked to inform their workplaces that they had been infected. Workplaces were then required to conduct their own risk assessments to assess close contacts onsite.    Although close contacts of confirmed COVID-19 cases would be contacted by Public Health to receive advice, the directions published on 26 December 2021 indicate that the State Government was reducing its involvement in contact tracing, and may have been unable to commit to comprehensive contact tracing for all COVID-19 cases.     The Tasmanian Government directions in place between 29 December 2021 and 31 December 2021 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. column106: According to the Tasmanian Government website, COVID-19 vaccines were available, free of charge, for all Tasmanians who were 12 years old and above. The Pfizer (Comirnaty) and Moderna (Spikevax) vaccines were available to those 12 years and over, and the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) vaccine was available to those 60 years and over.  As 90.87% of all Tasmanians 12 years old and above had been fully vaccinated as of 23 December 2021, the Tasmanian Government had the capacity to fulfill its universal vaccine policy.    Some immunocompromised individuals could receive a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine 2-6 months after their second dose. column115: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as of December 2021 and 5 January 2022), all people (excluding aged care facility residents) entering and remaining within a residential aged care facility were required to wear a surgical mask, and this included individuals under 12 years of age where practical.    Both unvaccinated and vaccinated individuals were allowed to enter residential aged care facilities, although unvaccinated individuals were required to obtain evidence of a negative PCR test taken within 72 hours prior to entering the facility. As of 5 January 2022, unvaccinated individuals could also enter aged care facilities with evidence of a negative RAT taken within 24 hours prior to entry. It is unclear exactly when this rule was introduced, due to the lack of archived versions of the webpage between 29 December 2021 and 5 January 2022.    Individuals with COVID-19 symptoms, those required to quarantine or isolate, as well as those who had come into contact with a confirmed or reasonably suspected COVID-19 case, were prohibited from entering aged care facilities. Staff were unable to work at residential aged care facilities if they had visited COVID-19 exposure sites in the past 14 days.    Staff working at residential aged care facilities were required to complete a screening checklist, where they were prohibited from working if they could not meet the above requirements for entering a residential aged care facility, and did not have a public health exemption.    Aside from the ability of unvaccinated visitors and staff to obtain a negative RAT taken within 24 hours before entry, which represented a relaxation of previous COVID-19 policy restrictions, the measures in place between 29 December 2021 and 5 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. column106: On 1 March 2021, it was reported that ‘a total of 100 COVID-19 vaccination doses were administered yesterday at hospital vaccination hubs across Victoria’, bringing the total number of vaccine doses administered in Victoria since the program started on Monday 22 February to 3862.  ‘The vaccines are being administered through hospital vaccination hubs managed by public health services. Hubs also manage several special outreach sites including at Melbourne Airport and the Port of Portland.  From today, 1 March 2021, vaccinations have commenced from the Bendigo and Ballarat hubs. These hubs will focus on public sector residential aged care residents throughout this week.’ Archived link: https://web.archive.org/web/20210508103904/https://www.dhhs.vic.gov.au/coronavirus-update-victoria-1-march-2021  See also dept of Health for prioritised groups, updated 22 February 2021: http://web.archive.org/web/20210224154002mp_/https://www.health.gov.au/initiatives-and-programs/covid-19-vaccines/getting-vaccinated-for-covid-19/when-will-i-get-a-covid-19-vaccine   Vaccination started in Victoria on 22 February 2021 with hospital vaccination hubs across Victoria.  “Victorians with the highest risk of exposure to COVID-19 are being prioritised for the vaccine, including Hotel Quarantine and Health Hotel workers, airport and port workers, and frontline health staff in COVID-19 screening clinics, specialist COVID-19 wards, Intensive Care Units, Emergency Departments, and more.  The vaccines are being administered through hospital vaccination hubs managed by public health services. Hubs also manage several special outreach sites including at Melbourne Airport and the Port of Portland.  Hubs will also deliver the vaccine to public sector residential aged care patients and workers, with the Commonwealth responsible for providing the vaccine to the private sector aged care and disability sectors.  All nine hospital vaccination hubs will commence operations over the coming weeks. […] Looking forward, we are working to deliver 40,000 to 50,000 vaccines over the next four weeks.”  Archived link: http://web.archive.org/web/20210509032251/https://www.dhhs.vic.gov.au/coronavirus-update-victoria-22-february-2021  People on the priority list include:  People at increased risk of exposure, infection and transmission of COVID-19, include:  •	health, aged care and the disability care workforce  •	aged and disability care residents, and  •	people in other higher risk settings, such as quarantine and border workers. column42: See part 4 (gatherings) of the linked document   http://web.archive.org/web/20210926131826/http://www.gazette.vic.gov.au/gazette/Gazettes2021/GG2021S256.pdf    Summary:  - Visiting other people's homes is not permitted, except for essential reasons (including obtaining necessary goods or services, for compassionate reasons, or for work or education). As an exception, you may nominate one person outside your household to form a "bubble", and allow this person to visit your home.  - May not organise gatherings with any other person in a public space, unless for: care or compassionate reasons; work or education; exercise with others from same household; obtaining necessary goods or services.   - May conduct weddings for people who will die soon, or would be deported from Australia if the wedding did not occur. column69: INTERNAL TRAVEL RESTRICTIONS Most restrictions on travel within Victoria were lifted beginning on June 18. These previous restrictions included a 25-km travel limit for greater Melbourne and a prohibition on travel from Melbourne to regional Victoria or vice versa.   See:  http://web.archive.org/web/20211001130516/http://www.gazette.vic.gov.au/gazette/Gazettes2021/GG2021S313.pdf.   INTERSTATE TRAVEL RESTRICTIONS - Victoria operates a travel permit system whereby regions of Australia and New Zealand are classified as green, orange, or red zones based on the level of COVID-19 transmission. All travellers (including those from green zones) must obtain a permit to enter Victoria, but only those coming from orange or red zones are subject to more onerous measures such as mandatory testing and isolation. Arrivals from orange zones must be tested within 72 hours and self-quarantine until a negative result, while arrivals from red zones are limited to Victorian residents (barring exemptions) and require 14 days of self-quarantine.   See  https://web.archive.org/web/20210617035912/https://www.coronavirus.vic.gov.au/victorian-travel-permit-system.  - From 6pm on June 17th, the LGAs of City of Sydney, Woollahra, and Waverley are upgraded from green zones to orange zones. Everywhere else in Greater Sydney, regional NSW, and the rest of Australia is a green zone.   See  https://web.archive.org/web/20210618003757/https://www.coronavirus.vic.gov.au/travel-updates.
column79: The Victorian Government continues to offer several debt/contract relief options for struggling Victorian households. column77: Individuals may be eligible for various types of income support. There are three main types. The 'COVID-19 Disaster Payment' is a lump sum payment to help workers unable to earn income due to a COVID-19 state or territory public health order. This may involve a lockdown, hotspot or movement restrictions. The 'Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment' and the 'Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19)' provides income support for those who are required to enter quarantine or isolation.     This is a continuation of the national policy response to COVID-19.    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004190443/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/subjects/getting-help-during-coronavirus-covid-19/if-you-need-payment

column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418. - The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220220083607/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments  https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment

column77: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. There is also a COVID-19 Disaster Payment, a lump sum payment for workers unable to earn an income due to state or territory public health orders (e.g. a lockdown). The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week. The following venues could only open if everyone was fully vaccinated, with density requirements in place:  	- Religious events and ceremonies  	- Physical recreation and sporting facilities  	- Beauty and personal care services  	- Real estate inspections and auctions  	- Some community facilities (e.g. libraries and studios)  	- Food and drink facilities  	- Arcades, casinos, and e-gaming facilities  	- Entertainment venues and events (e.g. music festivals)  	- Tours and tour transport    All retail venues (including retail betting venues) were open to all patrons with a density requirement of one person per 4 square metres. Accommodation services were open to everyone in a household and up to 10 additional people including dependents. Vaccination requirements did not apply to community sport. If vaccination status was not being checked at religious events, food and drink facilities, or real estate inspections, these venues were required to adhere to stricter density requirements.    Masks were mandatory indoors for everyone aged 12 years old and above, regardless of vaccination status. column42: A continuation of the existing policy, the following restrictions implemented by the Victorian Government remained in place between the 24th November and the 30th November.  For private gatherings;  •	There are no limits to the number of people you can gather with in your home or in public places (e.g. a park or a beach).  •	We strongly recommend that everyone who you are gathering with at your home or in a public place is fully vaccinated.  The following venues are closed to people who do not meet the vaccination requirements:  •	food and drink venues (e.g. restaurants and pubs)  •	nightlife venues (e.g. bars and nightclubs)  •	entertainment venues (e.g. cinemas, zoos)  •	events (e.g. festivals, fun runs and conferences)  •	tourism venues (e.g. walking tours, buses)  •	casinos/gaming venues and adult entertainment venues  If you don’t meet the vaccination requirements, you can’t enter these venues.  For weddings, funerals and worship, if vaccination status isn’t being checked, these events are restricted to one person per 4 sqm up to a maximum of 50 people per facility. column69: A continuation of the existing policy, the following restrictions implemented by the Victorian Government remained in place between the 24th November and the 30th November. column90: A continuation of the existing policy, the following restrictions implemented by the Victorian Government remained in place between the 24th November and the 30th November. column103: A continuation of the existing policy, the following restrictions implemented by the Victorian Government remained in place between the 24th November and the 30th November. column115: A continuation of the existing policy, the following restrictions implemented by the Victorian Government remained in place between the 24th November and 30th November.  •	You can visit a patient at a public, private, or denominational hospital, day procedure or multi-purpose health services centre:  •	if it is an end-of life visit  •	if the patient is ill with a life-threatening condition  •	to provide essential care and support necessary for the patient’s emotional and physical wellbeing  •	if the patient is under 18 and you are the patient's parent or guardian  •	if the patient has a mental illness or is living with dementia and you are their nominated person  •	if you are required to provide interpreter services  •	if you are required to support the patient upon their discharge  •	if the patient is pregnant or giving birth and you are their partner  •	if you are accompanying the patient to the emergency department, or  •	if you are accompanying the patient to an outpatient appointment.  Each patient can have up to two visitors at a time unless the dependants of a visitor (or patient in hospital) are in the visitor group and care for the dependants cannot be arranged.  You must not visit a hospital to see patients if you have tested positive to COVID-19, have had contact with someone who has COVID-19 in the previous 7 days if fully vaccinated and not a close contact, or in the previous 14 days if not fully vaccinated or a close contact, if you have COVID-19 symptoms, are waiting for a COVID-19 test result are under 16 unless you're providing end-of-life support, visiting a patient with a life-threatening condition or related to the patient, have permission from the hospital or Chief Health Officer to visit or if you are an overseas traveller or an international aircrew service worker who just arrived in Victoria.  A close contact is someone who has spent more than 4 hours in a home, accommodation premises or care facility with someone who has COVID-19.  Staff and visitors must wear a mask unless an exemption applies.  You should contact the hospital before visiting as they may have additional requirements, conditions, or restrictions for visitors. This information may also be found on their website.  •	Visiting care facilities  Each resident in a care facility is permitted up to five visitors per day, including dependants.  Visitors must sign a declaration upon entry to state that they have not been in contact with a confirmed case in the past 7 days if fully vaccinated and if not a household contact, or the last 14 days if not fully vaccinated or if a household contact. column88: "If you have any of the symptoms of COVID-19, however mild, you should seek advice and get tested.  People with no symptoms (asymptomatic) can also be tested for COVID-19 in very specific circumstances:  -If you are a close contact exposed to someone known to have COVID-19.  -If you are a returned international traveller.   -If you are due to have surgery or a planned hospital stay.  -If you are part of a targeted testing program across an industry or group.    Asymptomatic people in the community who want to check if they have COVID-19 should not get a PCR test.  They should opt for Rapid Antigen Tests, and if they are currently unavailable, should continue to monitor for symptoms and stay COVIDSafe.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220105233434/https://www.coronavirus.vic.gov.au/where-get-tested-covid-19  https://web.archive.org/web/20220105233434/https://www.coronavirus.vic.gov.au/where-get-tested-covid-19
column103: "Wearing a mask is required for everyone aged 8 and above in all indoor settings in Victoria. Exceptions apply to wearing face masks: when in a home, when consuming food or drink, or when receiving beauty services.    Wearing a mask is also required in the following settings:  -On public transport, in taxis/rideshare services, in tourism vehicles and on commercial flights.  -At an airport.  -While attending an event that has 30,000 or more patrons present, unless you are seated outdoors at the event.  -While visiting a hospital or care facility.  -After being tested for COVID-19 and awaiting results, other than as part of surveillance testing.  -If the person has COVID-19 or is a contact, and is leaving the premises in line with quarantine, isolation or testing requirements.  -International passenger arrivals and international aircrew services workers who are in direct transit to their place of self-quarantine in Victoria and who leave their vehicle, or who are in self-quarantine and leave to undertake permitted essential services.    Strongly recommend wearing a mask if you can’t physically distance, even if you are outdoors, have any symptoms, or if you are with people who may be vulnerable to COVID-19.  Always carry a mask when leaving home."    https://web.archive.org/web/20220104154853/https://www.coronavirus.vic.gov.au/face-masks-when-wear-face-mask

column115: As stated on the Victorian Government website:  "Each resident in a care facility is permitted up to five visitors per day, including dependants. column24: As announced on the WA Government's website and a media statement by the WA Premier on 13 May 2021, WA (including the Perth and Peel regions) was to return to 'pre-lockdown life' on 15 May 2021. column77: -	People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 7 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments.

column77: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. There is also a COVID-19 Disaster Payment, a lump sum payment for workers unable to earn an income due to state or territory public health orders (e.g. a lockdown). The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. column24: As of 23 Dec 2021, workplace restrictions across the Perth and Peel regions are tightening. The WA Government announced that from 23 Dec 2021, in Perth and Peel, only licensed hospitality venues may serve food and beverages, and this must be consumed seated. In addition, nightclubs must be closed, and certain high-risk music events cannot go ahead. Masks must also be worn in all indoor spaces, which includes indoor workplaces.  For areas outside of Perth and Peel, no businesses are closed, but they must continue to provide a COVID Safety plan and maintain a contact register. column33: As of 23 Dec 2021, event restrictions across the Perth and Peel regions are tightening. The WA Government announced that from 23 Dec 2021, in Perth and Peel, music events with more than 500 patrons are prohibited. People attending large events that are not high-risk music events are encouraged to wear a mask (and must wear a mask if indoors).  For areas outside of Perth and Peel, public events may go ahead without capacity limits, but events with more than 500 patrons must complete a COVID Event Checklist or Plan. column42: As of 23 Dec 2021, restrictions across Perth and Peel regions are tightening, although the gathering restrictions remain similar. The WA Government announced that from 23 Dec 2021, in Perth and Peel, gatherings of more than 500 people that involve music (or related activities, such as singing or dancing) are prohibited. Events with more than 500 patrons that do not include music may go ahead, but require a COVID Event Checklist or Plan.   For areas outside of Perth and Peel, gatherings and events may go ahead without capacity limits, but events with more than 500 patrons must complete a COVID Event Checklist or Plan. column51: As of 23 Dec 2021, restrictions across Perth and Peel regions are tightening. column60: As of 23 Dec 21, there continues to be no stay at home requirements across WA. column103: As of 23 Dec 2021, masks continue to be required in some public spaces across WA. According to the WA Government, from 23 Dec 2021, restrictions are tightening in Perth and Peel, which means masks are required in all indoor spaces, and on public transport, taxi, and ride share services (link 1). For regions outside of Perth and Peel, according to Healthdirect (an Australian Government website), masks are required in airports, aircrafts and when transporting a person under quarantine (link 2). Masks are also required to be worn by quarantine centre workers inside aged care facilities across WA (link 1). column115: As of 23 Dec 2021, there continues to be narrow protection of elderly people across WA, despite easing of restrictions in Perth and Peel. Since 22 September 2021, when the WA Emergency Officer signed off on it, people across WA can not enter aged care facilities if they: have returned from overseas in the past 14 days, have been a close contact in the past 14 days, have any COVID-19 symptoms, or have not had an up-to-date flu vaccine (link 1). The WA Government announced further restrictions on Perth and Peel from 23 Dec 2021 (link 2). Staff and visitors must wear masks indoors, including in aged care facilities. Quarantine centre workers must also remain 1.5m away from other people when visiting aged care facilities. Archived weblinks: 1. https://web.archive.org/web/20211027095329/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-09/Visitors-to-Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-Directions-No8.pdf 2. https://web.archive.org/web/20211228134843/https://www.wa.gov.au/government/covid-19-coronavirus/covid-19-coronavirus-what-you-can-and-cant-do

column15: As of 24 Dec 2021, there continues to be some restrictions on schools across WA. As published on the Healthdirect website, and the WA Department of Education website, the WA Government announced that all students are expected to attend school, except for those students medically referred to learn from home.  Schools are required to maintain daily hygiene. If there is a confirmed COVID-19 case at a school, the decision to close a school is based on expert advice from the WA Health Department’s Chief Health Officer (Links 1 & 2). This is a continuation of existing policies.  Also, COVID-19 restrictions were tightened on 23 Dec 2021 in the Perth and Peel regions by the WA Government, which includes mandatory mask wearing indoors (which includes schools, excluding primary school students) (link 3). column69: As of 24 Dec 2021, there continues to be restrictions on internal movement into WA. This means that, on 24 Dec 2021, only essential travellers from Victoria and NSW (and all from other states) are permitted to enter WA (with quarantine). Also, entry into some remote Aboriginal communities is restricted to residents and essential workers (link 2). column106: Between 1 August 2021 and 29 August 2021, both Oxford AstraZeneca and Pfizer vaccines were being administered. According to the AHPPC on 26 July 2021, if there are Delta cases in the community a risk assessment will be undertaken by the jurisdiction that will consider the measures that need to be applied commensurate with the risk. AHPPC recognises the serious impact school closures have on all children and the need for the response to be proportionate to the risk of transmission in the school setting. During closures, vulnerable students and children of essential workers need to have continued access to onsite education. AHPPC continues to emphasise the importance of COVIDSafe plans and principles being embedded in school operations. When there are no local cases of COVID-19, standard plans include ensuring that; students and staff with symptoms do not attend school, visitors to the school are registered such as through QR codes. There needs to be importance placed on hand and respiratory hygiene along with good ventilation, regular cleaning and disinfection of the environment.    According to the Australian Government's webpage updated on 9 September 2021, the Corminaty (Pfizer) and Spikevax (Moderna) COVID-19 vaccines are approved and  recommended for people aged 12 and older. But it is not mandatory for students to get vaccinated. Therefore, it should be reported as 0. column77: The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those who lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those who lose 20 or more hours per week. The $750 weekly payment week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week.(http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).     The COVID-19 Disaster Payment automatic weekly payment will stop available when the states and territories reach 70% full vaccination for population aged 16 and above.     Apart from that, the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. column77: -	People who cannot work due to COVID-19 related reasons may be eligible to receive income support from the Australian Government.  -	The COVID-19 Disaster Payment is available to people who cannot attend work because they live or work in a Commonwealth-designated COVID-19 hotspot. The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week (http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours).   -	The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn. As of 7 October 2021, only NSW and the ACT had reached the 70% threshold, and no jurisdictions had reached the 80% threshold.  -	The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for people who cannot work because they are required to isolate due to COVID-19, or are caring for someone who is required to isolate. The payment is $1500 for each 14-day isolation period, which is more than half the median fortnightly income of $2418.  -	The eligibility criteria for these payments make no mention of formal or informal employment, with all workers who lost significant income due to lockdowns or isolation requirements entitled to receive support.  -	See http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments.

column77: The Australian Government continues to provide income support to formal workers - the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment - to households who cannot work due to quarantine, self-isolation, or caring for someone with COVID-19. There is also a COVID-19 Disaster Payment, a lump sum payment for workers unable to earn an income due to state or territory public health orders (e.g. a lockdown). The payment was $200 per week for those who are already receiving income support and lose at least 8 hours a week, $450 per week for those not already receiving income support and lose 8-20 hours a week, and $750 per week for those not already receiving income support who lose 20 or more hours per week. The maximum payment amount of $750 per week is more than half the median income, which is $1209 per week. The Government began phasing out the COVID-19 Disaster Payment when states and territories reached 70% full vaccination rate among the 16+ population. At 70 percent vaccination rate, automatic renewal of payments would end, and at 80 percent the payments would be gradually withdrawn.     http://web.archive.org/web/20220121014642/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-work-hours    http://web.archive.org/web/20220119223147/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2122/Quick_Guides/COVID-19DisasterPayments for information on these payments    https://web.archive.org/web/20211001040822/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/individuals/services/centrelink/covid-19-disaster-payment

Effective immediately, on 27/November/2021, anyone who is not a citizen or permanent resident of Australia, or their immediate family including parents of citizens, and who have been in African countries where the Omicron variant has been detected and spread – within the past 14 days – will not be able to enter Australia. column15: According to the statement released by AHPPC on 15 November 2021 schools should remain open whenever possible. They have introduced three principles that schools need to follow in order to minimize transmission when schools are open.   "Each of these principles has actions that should be considered when planning re-opening of schools noting that multiple steps will need to be taken and that these will need to be tailored by individual schools to be most effective.  Measures that are implemented should be evaluated for effect, cost-effectiveness, feasibility, sustainability and adverse consequences." column74: People must show evidence that they have been vaccinated, at least 7 days prior to international travel into or out of Australia, with a vaccine approved or recognised by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA). Additionally, the Australian Government has announced new border security measures to protect Australians from the Omicron COVID-19 variant. Effective immediately, on  nov 27, anyone who is not a citizen or permanent resident of Australia, or their immediate family including parents of citizens, and who have been in African countries where the Omicron variant has been detected and spread – within the past 14 days – will not be able to enter Australia.
